--- 帖子 #1259 ---
Basics in Stophunting

Hello dear subscribers,

The big players have so much money that they can move the course massively within seconds. In the following article, I described why that doesn't make sense for the Big Boys.

Identification of the big players

For this reason, the big players rely on collecting ask or bid in the sideways phases that is made available by a wide variety of market participants. In an accumulation phase, Ask is collected (cause) in order to push the price up in the medium term. (Effect) while bid is being collected in the distribution phase (cause) to push the price down in the medium term. (Effect). Therefore, a trader should analyze what is bought within an equilibrium. Important: When exiting the market, the big players do not sell their ask or bid in one block. Ask can only be sold if many market participants continue to expect rising prices. Therefore, a big player in the rising market sells his ask in small quantities and tries not to slow the price up. The advantage: the course continues to rise and the big player receives even better prices when exiting.

Market orders are transactions that should be executed as quickly as possible at the current or market price. Conversely, a limit order specifies the maximum or minimum price at which you want to buy or sell. As we already know, limit orders represent liquidity in the market. However, since there is a bid and ask spread, these limit orders never meet to trigger a market movement. The market buy orders (demand) hits the sell limit orders (offer) and the market sell orders (offer) hits the buy limit orders (demand). If a price is pushed upwards, many market oders are usually traded, with absorption, additional limit orders are added to a price level to stop the market orders. Market orders can also be triggered by a TP or stops.

A crucial point is the identification of ask and bid. Ask comes into the market because someone buys the euro or sells the dollar. Bid comes into the market because someone buys the dollar or sells the euro. If a strong bullish candle unexpectedly emerges in a downward trend, this does not necessarily mean that someone is buying the euro and the price will continue to rise. It could also mean that a big player leaves his position and sells his dollars. Then the price would very likely not rise immediately, but rather run into a sideways range. How price movements occur and the spread changes can be read here:

The wrong truth?

Resistance zones

In the post: "The wrong truth?" I showed that randomly drawn resistance zones work amazingly well. However, this is a pure coincidence and has nothing to do with actual resistance zones. We traders often try to sort a random price trend using horizontal, vertical or trend lines to derive a future forecast. But what we draw there gives us a truth that does not really exist. The first question we have to ask ourselves: Do resistance zones only happen by chance and how should we deal with them?

Resistance zones actually exist and, as a rule, they do not arise accidentally. The big players know that traders like to work with Fibonacci zones, moving averages (EMA 200) as well as resistance and support zones. With the help of these zones, the retail traders make important trading decisions. When a price stops three times in a row at the same price level, many traders assume that it is a very strong resistance zone that cannot be broken. The opposite is true, however, because it would be no problem for the big players to break through this resistance zone. But they make us believe that it is a strong zone. The next time the price comes to this zone, a large number of traders may take short positions and place their stops above this supposedly strong resistance zone.

Even if some traders assume that this resistance zone has been initiated, speculate on a long position and put their stops below the resistance zone, it is no good idea. The big player initially pushes the price down sharply, where its buy limit orders intercept the triggered stops of the traders. Now the big player is able to buy Ask even cheaper before pushing the price up. As soon as the big players push the price above their fake resistance zone and catch the traders' stops, the price is pushed further upwards, because at this moment further ask comes into the market. In this case, the short and long traders were switched off before the big player implemented his strategy.

Resistance zones are therefore an important tool for quickly getting liquidity. Especially in the sideways markets, people like to work with these resistance zones to collect bid or ask unnoticed. When you identify a typical resistance zone, you should always ask yourself first what the big players are up to?

Trends

A trend is described as a particularly profound and sustainable course development. For me, a trend is just a price trend that can develop in the opposite direction at any time. There can be endless discussions about trends, although there will always be different views.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Let us first look at the EURUSD in the monthly chart. We see here a price development of the past 588 months. The two green lines clearly indicate an upward trend since 1971, while the two red lines clearly indicate a downward trend from 2010. Is it a major upward trend and at the same time a minor downward trend? Is that really true and how does this information help us?

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

We switch to the EURUSD daily chart. We have been in a downward trend since February 2018, and we have been in an upward trend since September 2019. Another view is, that we are still in a downtrend and the new uptrend will be confirmed, when reached the last high of February 2018. But even if the high of Feb 2018 is overcome, it does not automatically mean that the price continues to go up. What is the benefit of looking at a trend for our future trading decisions? Due to different time units, the consideration of different trends is completely understandable, the main question is which trends apply to the individual trader and which future decision he will make with this knowledge.

An upward trend is identified if ever higher highs and higher lows are formed in the price trend. Downward trends are identified when steadily falling lows and constantly falling highs are formed in the price trend. Big players also know these rules very well and use them to obtain the necessary liquidity. Let's look at a simple example.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The case described here is only intended as an example. Depending on the trading style and strategy, there are different approaches.

Point A

The upward trend ends here, but this is not yet apparent to a trader at this point. First the course runs to point B.

Point B

When the price reached point B, it is still not clear whether it is already a downward trend because the price could go up again and form a new high. The price initially goes up a bit and then forms a new low at point C.

Point C

After a new low has been formed at point C, this is a confirmed downward trend for many traders and they first wait for the pullback to find a good start. This entry then takes place at point F and the stop comes via the last high at point D.

Point E

After the course has formed a new low and has run to point E, the stop is pulled to point F. In some cases, stops are pulled faster regardless of highs or lows.

Point G

After the course has formed a new low and has run to point G, the stop is moved to point H. Due to the stronger price trend at point H, some traders have already been kicked out of the market.

Point I

The course has now reached point I and the stop is dragged to point J.

Point K

From point I, the price is pushed into zone K and triggers some stops by the traders. After that, the price continues down to point L. Some traders believe, the price will go further down and starts a short position at point K. Some traders believe it is going up and starts a long position at point L.

Point M

Now the price is pushed to point M and stops further traders. On this occasion, the big players are able to purchase larger orders from bid to push the price further down to point N. At the same time, the long traders who entered the market at point L are stopped. The short traders from point F onwards must hand over winnings to the big players.

This example clearly shows that the big players are trying to stop all different trader groups or to reduce their profits. It is a great art to ensure that neither scalpers, day traders, swing traders nor position traders come to a noteworthy result at the same time. Of course, we have to take into account the different stops of the individual market participants.

Since the big players are unable to bring their positions directly into the market, they are forced to look for suitable liquidity. This liquidity is immediately released as soon as the traders' stops are triggered. For this reason, it is important to recognize where the individual stops of the traders are. As soon as you identify these stops, you can use it to estimate a further course of the course. As I wrote in my last post, stop identification is not a guarantee of successful trading. Based on future data, we can see what the big players buy or sell within these stops. But we will deal with this in more detail in our Project No. 10. First of all, it is important to identify possible stops in order to find out where the greatest liquidity is in the market. This shows us the direction in which the big players are building their trade. We have to keep in mind that stops are moved, which makes it easier for the big players to achieve this liquidity (stops) quickly with a counter trend (course of the point G to point H). For a better overview, the indicators that I published in my last post will help you. If you click on the link, you will come directly to the article and can download the associated indicators.

Supporting indicators for Project No.9

First, draws possible stops of the individual long and short traders and decides which liquidity could be the next target. First of all, this gives you a rough overview with which you already get a lot of information. The identification of different stops is a process that does not work straight away and requires experience. It is therefore completely normal for the first results take a little longer.

I wish you a successful trading week

best regards

Michael

Margin hunting

Hello Js3mwtRc,

This is an interesting question that I can only answer emotionally, because I have not yet been confronted with it.

Let us first consider the Forex market. 85% of sales come from the big players, 10% from the smaller institutional traders and the remaining 5% from the retail traders. The big players and the majority of the institutional dealers work almost exclusively with their own funds, a margin does not apply here. It is different with most retail traders. Many work with levers and the broker demands a margin for this. This security is intended to ensure that the holder of a buy or sell position can fulfill his obligation if the development of the course should develop to his disadvantage. If the existing kontract cannot absorb a negative development of the trade and a margin call is ignored, the positions can be closed by the broker for security. However, a margin call is an extremely rare exception for most traders. I haven't had a margin call in the past 10 years. In addition, most positions are hedged with stops, and should there be a sharp fall in prices, 95% of traders in Europe are only liable with their account deposits. Therefore, I don't believe that big players target an account's entire margin if a stop comes into play beforehand. The big players earn $ 400 million a day in Forex, primarily through stop hunting. It's a very rewarding business, but it's wiser to keep retail traders going than to flatten them. Why should you slaughter a cow that gives 50 liters of milk every day?

I am glad that this blog helps you and I wish you continued success with our new project Nr.9.

--- 帖子 #1266 ---
Margin hunting

Hello Js3mwtRc,

A futures margin is also a security deposit, that is required from the broker, when trading futures and or when using automatic futures trading systems. The sum of the margin minus netted gains and losses of all open futures positions held represents the equity of a margin account. There are two types of future margin, firstly the initial margin and secondly the maintenance margin. The initial margin is due when a position is entered. The maintenance margin can be called up by means of a margin call if the existing kontract cannot compensate for a negative development of the trade.

If you finance your contract in the future from your own funds, there is no margin. Futures are also leverage instruments because investors only purchase them on a margin and initially require little capital. The margin in the future is therefore also a security deposit that a broker requires when you enter a trading position. This affects the areas of futures and CFDs, because you do not buy or sell a security, but enter into a contract, i.e. an obligation. And it starts exactly the moment you go long or short with the future or CFD, at the price that is then available in the underlying. There is no actual purchase price and no transfer of a security to your portfolio. However, there is always the risk, that only a small amount of liquidity will be invested, but in the event of a loss, due to the additional margin requirements, more liquidity will flow away than the trader can handle.

If you go long with a contract in the Euro FX Future, the book value of your portfolio increases by $ 6.25 for every tick that the Euro FX gains. If the Euro FX suddenly fell 100 ticks, you would lose $ 625. By doing this, the broker protects itself against losses that it would otherwise have to bear. If the big player was targeting the margin, it would have to be ensured that you didn't use a stop. But also in the futures market, stops are usually used and if you place a 10-tick stop on 1 lot, the risk is limited to $ 62.50. The only way the big player would have is to motivate you to extend your stop. However, shortly before your stop, he would have to steer the course in the opposite direction again. So I cannot imagine that margin hunting could be a sensible strategy.

I recommend you first deal with the Stophunting in our project No. 9. The knowledge gained from this will help you to be less stopped in the future.

Stophunting, Project No. 9 starts

Supporting indicators for Project No.9

Basics in Stophunting

I wish you a successful trading week

Price manipulation

[quote=Js3mwtRc;12714467]{quote} I know you are right, no one can move the market against its position,

Hello Js3mwtRc,

In the area of price manipulation, the first step is always the decisive liquidity in the market. In addition to Stophunting, our new project sheds light on precisely this liquidity, which initiates interesting turnarounds. The hunt for liquidity continues until it is exhausted, after which a counter-trend begins. We will talk about these manipulations in more detail and see some examples.

To your question:

You do not need to perform cumbersome arithmetic operations with the calculator to see if you can afford a position from the margin or when that security will expire. All of this is done for you. Your order mask in the future, shows how high the margin must be for a particular position when you enter the order. If your free stock in the brokerage account is not sufficient, such an order will not be implemented at all. With a margin of $ 5,000 and equity of 10,000 euros, you would have $ 5,000 leeway, after which your broker would ask you to add capital to the account to replenish the margin. But a stop loss should always be used to protect the margin.

If you do not have a future account, you may be able to download an analysis tool from the Internet. It is a system for calculating the margin requirements for futures and options. Just look for "Span file" and make sure that there are no costs for this tool.

Future data

Hello Dcrs, hello dear subscriber,

First of all, thank you for your contribution and your views on the market. At first glance, the stock market data in the futures market are very simple, we have the price, the time, the volume and the liquidity. From this you can create bid and ask, the volume delta, footprint charts, the heat map, a volume profile, the DOM, the time and sales list and many more views. We have been dealing with these different representations for over a year and tried to implement the information available about them. The trick is to filter the data, compare it with each other and present it in such a way that it shows you exactly what is currently happening in the market. With my software, I am able to read this data very explicitly and present it effectively, but there is still a great challenge to see the market as I would like it to be. Since the market orders move the market, I initially thought that these orders are the decisive factor in the market. The opposite is true, however, because liquidity is the much more crucial factor. And strangely, we get the least information about it. I will write a detailed report on this at the weekend, so please be patient.

I only use the futures data passively because the forex market provides 100 times the liquidity, my security is highest in this market and the price movements are 5 times better graded. In the Forex market you can better recognize the currency strength, read out the price strength better and identify possible stops more precisely. The cash market is the lead wolf, however, apart from the price and the time, it does not provide the crucial information about what happens within a candle. And this information is the key to being more likely to get a competitive edge. And it is precisely this market advantage that decides between profit and loss.

Many traders believe that the market is very simple, but that is a big mistake. If this were the case, EA's would make above-average profits in all market phases in the long term and the big players would not invest billions of dollars in analysts, their IT technology, algorithms and their traders. In addition, not over 90% of all retail traders would lose their money in the long term. These are clear facts that should not be overlooked. Of course you can make money with a price chart, which I have practiced myself for over 10 years, but primarily because I acted during the accumulation and distribution phase, where the big players first had to collect their bid or ask. This strategy requires an experience of at least 5-7 years and and very few traders have this time. If you add the futures data in parallel, you can achieve your profitable trading much faster. The participants in the futures market have a 1: 6 chance, the participants in the forex market have a 1: 19 chance. This is primarily due to the existing data that is available.

The Forexcharts are ideal for identifying possible stops. Stops mean liquidity, which is the decisive factor for the Big Player.

--- 帖子 #1280 ---
Liquidity versus volume

Hello dear subscribers,

First of all I would like to describe our project No. 9 and 10 in more detail. So that you have an idea of what to expect, we first go a little deeper into the market.

Due to the different languages here at FF, there may be misunderstandings when translating this article, which I would be happy to explain or correct in detail. I do not claim to be free of errors. Today's contribution should not be understood as instruction or correct market presentation, but should only reflect my view of the market. We are in a project that is only used to generate market advantages. Before we take a closer look at Stophunting, I would like to address an important point that we have noticed in the past few days.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

As we know, price movements in the market result from the active market orders meeting the passive limit orders. On the left side we see the buy limit orders (point A) and on the right side the sell limit orders (point B). These orders represent liquidity in the market and are separated from each other by the spread ask and bid. Only through the limit orders alone will there be no market movement. The liquidity is in the market and is waiting for the market orders. As soon as a buy market orders comes into the market, it meets the sell limit orders (point B). You can read about how these market movements develop here.

Identification of the big players

The wrong truth?

Point C shows the cumulative sell market orders of the first ten levels in the DOM and Point D shows the cumulative buy market orders, which are each shown in lot. While there are 856 lots in the first ten stages of the sell market orders in the Euro FX market, this should be around 85,600 in the Forex market, since the Forex market is 100 times larger. However, this is only a rough estimate, since the actual Forex volume is only visible to the big players. At Point E we see spoofing in the area of the buy limit orders and at Point F the spoofing of the sell limit orders. This shows how many limit orders are added or subtracted. At Point G we see the total volume on the left and next to it the number of trades that were responsible for this volume. On the right side of the chart is the Times and Sales list, with the display of Level I + II. The individual market orders run in from top to bottom under the name "Vol". At Point H we recognize 11 and 21 lots that came onto the market. These are cumulative orders that are summarized within a thousandth of a second and disguise their actual size. At point I we see the strength of the liquidity at the time of execution.

First of all, I would like to take a closer look at the cumulative orders. A cumulative order is a large order that is divided into small pieces and is difficult to recognize in the DOM. It is broken down into smaller orders by an automated program to hide the actual orders amount. Another advantage that arises from this: By hiding their volume, this orders reduces possible strong price movements, as well as the change in supply and demand. This means that a big player with a large volume comes onto the market without the other participants noticing. In principle it is also a kind of iceberg orders, however the correct iceberg orders are placed in the limit.

Let's look at a specific example of the cumulative orders.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The advantage of the bid and ask display in a 1 tick chart (point A) is that each tick can be produced by a maximum of one market participant. First of all, I would like to clear up a general misunderstanding. In the lower chart we see a representation of bid and ask. At first glance, it looks like it's an indicator. However, the volume is not an indicator; like the price, it is a fixed part of trading and, unlike indicators, does not have to be offset. This representation is processed from the current real-time data of the exchange, so such a representation is not available for the MT4 in the Forex market. In the chart we see a 40 lot order, this 40 lot could only have been placed by one market participant. However, it is difficult to identify cumulative orders in a 1-tick chart.

At Point B we see the time and sales list at that time. If the individual orders are not displayed cumulatively, it is almost impossible to keep a close eye on the rapidly falling numbers. However, you have the option of accumulating the order within the time and sales list and sorting it within a thousandth of a second. This allows you to initially identify cumulative orders. For a rough overview, you can use a small trick by opening a 1 second chart. In the charts at Point C we can see that over 400 lot bids have entered the market within 2 seconds. Then I would have to look explicitly at the cumulative time and sales list to see exactly what happened there.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

For the identification of the cumulative orders, I first put together my own presentation. At point A we see the non-cumulative market sell order, this is a market order that is visible to all participants in the market. Point B shows the cumulative orders between 10 and 20 lots, Point C the cumulative orders between 20 and 30 lot and Point D the cumulative orders from 31 lot. On the far left we see the spread tape showing the delta and on the far right the accumulated market orders divided by ask and bid. In the DOM we see the limit orders, the cumulative spoofing and the processed market orders. With the respective times, I am able to recognize whether cumulative orders come into the market one after the other in a certain rhythm. In addition, I work with acoustic tones that inform me immediately as soon as large, cumulative orders appear. The tones differ between bid and ask, which is a great help that I can recommend to everyone.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The two most popular tools in volume trading are the volume profile and the footprintchart, let's start with the volume profile. This representation is initially much better than a price chart in Forex, because it is not about indicators, but the volume that is a fixed part of trading and does not have to be calculated first. First, the volume shows the number of contacts traded in a certain period or at a certain price. In the charts we see three decisive factors: on the left the horizontal volume of the entire contract, in the M 30 candles the horizontal volume at each price level and at the bottom the volume delta, i.e. the net result from bid and ask. This allows you to determine within a candle where the highest volume has taken place. There are an infinite number of theories and approaches for deriving trading decisions from them, but these are too imprecise for me. The first point is that a volume contains both bid and ask. This shows me that at this moment a lot of buyers and sellers have met and that this price level could be an important zone. However, deriving further courses from this is a major challenge in my view, since I have to work with unclear information. If after a large volume, the price keeps going up, it doesn't necessarily mean that it will remain bullish. The much more crucial point is liquidity and we cannot see this liquidity in this presentation. Basically a very good alternative to forex data, but in my view much too imprecise and too slow.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The footprint charts have become more important in recent years because you have the opportunity to look into the individual price levels of a candle. However, we initially only see the executed market orders in this footprint chart. It is advantageous that you can filter the imbalance in bid and ask in orders to identify the more aggressive market participants. At point A, I once highlighted the more aggressive market participants, but this is not concrete help to derive a trade from it. Resistance zones are often drawn based on the imbalance, which I can only advise against.

We know that a purchase will only take place if there is a seller at the same time. A market order can only enter the market if it meets a limit order at the same time. The footprint chart shows the bid order on the left and the ask order on the right. If a number appears in the footprint chart, it also means that this market order has triggered a limit order. A buy market order can be the purchase of the euro or the sale of the dollar. When I go short in EURUSD, I buy the dollar first. I need Bid for that. Of course, I also sell the euro at the same time. When I get out of my position, I sell the dollar and need Ask. For this, however, someone has to be willing to take my ask from me. That means there must be market participants who believe that the dollar will continue to fall. If there is no buyer, the price goes up and reduces my profit.

I swapped the color of the Bid and Ask in the footprint chart below, as a sell market order (bid) meets a buy limit order (ask). At point B we see that a 14 lot sell market orders (bid) triggered a total of 14 lot ask in the buy limit orders. Point C shows an 18 lot buy market orders (ask) that triggered a total of 18 lots in the sell limit orders. And that's exactly the problem. We can see the market orders in the footprint chart, but not the triggered limit orders. And it is precisely this aspect that is an excellent opportunity for big players to enter the market unnoticed.

The footprint chart can be used well to optimally display the market orders coming into the market. This is a bit more complex in DOM, since the market orders always refer to at least one day. In order to have a good overview, you have to delete the old market orders in the DOM so that the new orders are clearly displayed again. So the footprint chart has a certain justification for me, but from a completely different perspective.

Absorption

Absorption is the magic word, but it is a fallacy to believe that absorption is always so strong that it slows down the price and keeps it at a price level for a long time. We'll look at a few examples in a moment. Let's stay with absorption. First of all, we know that the market orders eat into the limit orders. If the liquidity of the sell limit orders is low and the buyers of the buy market orders are very aggressive, the sell limit orders are literally eaten up and the price goes up. Suddenly the upward course is stopped. There are two options for this: either the active market orders become weaker or the passive limit orders become stronger. If the passive limit orders get stronger, you can not see that in the DOM in most cases. You can see that spoofing is counting up, but in principle only the maximum ask that the market orders provides can be absorbed. How does it work in practice? As soon as the price reaches a certain price level, the algorithms of the big players start to push new limit orders again and again. The total visible amount of the limit orders does not change. However, you can see that the executed market orders count up while the price is not moving up. What makes things more difficult, however, is that absorption rarely takes place at one price level, but at several. There are two reasons for this. If a price stayed at a price level even though buyers are very aggressive, buyers would eventually realize that something was wrong and might get out. This would end the absorption and the price would run down due to the many dropouts. In principle, the art is that buyers don't realize that they're being absorbed. This attracts other buyers, who can then be absorbed in peace. The more buyers come into the market, the better. If the price is then suddenly pushed down, the entire longtrader stops are triggered and the price continues to accelerate downwards.

The price is solely the result of liquidity, volume and time. This is a crucial point that is very important. This is proof that the price has nothing to do with the value of a currency. The problem in the forex market is that we don't get volume and liquidity data there. How should I solve this equation with the price and the time alone? This automatically means that price indicators don't work and actually don't help us. When I work with the price in Forex, I deal with the effect without knowing the cause. The high loss rates of retail traders show where this leads.

For me, time is an absolute side aspect, volume is decisive and liquidity is even more crucial. Resistance zones are only important for retail traders, they do not exist for big players. Absorption via passive liquidity creates resistance zones that the big players never pay attention to because they create them themself. In an accumulation and distribution phase, however, that's another story. There, the resistance zones have clear authorization to collect the required ask or bid. However, they are always created by the big players in order to present a wrong picture of supply and demand.

In order to be profitable within a sideways phase, one should be a scalper and at the same time accept higher fees from the broker. In these phases, the support and resistance zones work as long as you stay within this zone. If you try to trade in the outbreak, you will fail in most cases. This has been my great luck in recent years since I was tradingwith theprice in the equilibrium.

Retail traders usually enter the market with a limit or market order, and profitable exit usually takes place through an immediate closing of the position (market order) or with a take profit (buy / sell limit order). A stopploss is also a market order. The big players cannot buy their large positions immediately, so they collect their positions in the form of cumulative orders. Different order types and algorithms are used, such as MOC, LOC, OCA, MTL, FOK, IOC and many more. In order to push the price strongly in one direction, the big players also work with market orders, provided that there is sufficient liquidity on the market. However, you can create this liquidity yourself beforehand by pretending to the market that the price is going down. As a result, more traders position themselves on the sell limit side and the big players can buy into the strong liquidity with their market orders. I'll show you equal a specific example, from last Friday. As I have noticed, these movements are usually not so sustainable. It is interesting, however, that many sellers actually drive the price up because they provide the big players with enough ask.

In slide # 3 we can see a lot of cumulative market orders, but my guess is that most of these cumulative market orders do not come from the big players. I believe that most big players use limit orders to get in and out as this guarantees the best price. Now everyone will ask, how can you move the market with limit orders? Answer: Not at all, because that is not necessary at first. Let's take a closer look at the market first. The strong movements make up only about 25% of the market, while the market moves in a sideways phase in about 75% of the time. This means that the big players deal with getting in and out 75% of the time and use 25% of the time to push the course in a certain direction. However, this statement can only be made across the board, as there are different market situations.

If the big players with limit orders absorb the market orders of institutional and retail traders, no software can actually determine this. This is a classic iceberg order. We only see the market order, but we know that they activate a limit order at the same time. If the big players absorb the market orders with their limit orders, they must pay attention to the following. The limit orders in the DOM must not be noticeable, so algorithms always have to push new limit Orders unnoticed and at the same time make sure that the market does not stall. This means that the big players primarily need as many market orders as possible at one price level. And where can you find them? Answer: In triggered stops. That is exactly why the big players concentrate on Stophunting. There, large quantities of market orders are released within seconds, which you only have to collect. And it is exactly this collection that takes place in secret, so that most market participants do not even realize what is happening there.

Now there is only one challenge for the big players, that is the queue for order execution. In the market, all orders are executed according to the "first come, first served" principle. So you line up in a queue and wait for its execution. If you place a limit order shortly before a possible execution, there is a high probability that you will have to queue up. Due to the market conditions, the big players place their limit orders in the market early, sometimes an hour beforehand. As soon as other market participants delete limit orders at this price level, they immediately add new limits. This ensures in most cases that the big players are the first in the queue. This is even more dramatic in the forex market because 12 banks control 85% of the market. You can guess three times who is always the first in the queue. For us retail traders above an ECN broker, this is less of a problem, since enough liquidity or bid and ask are available to be executed immediately. Execution problems can only occasionally occur in very volatile phases.

The goal of a trader is to look at the order flow in the market to see how the price responds to it. This automatically results in a market advantage and this market advantage leads to a higher probability of winning. In my opinion, with order flow or volume, we are unable to learn the truth about the current situation in the market. In 75% of the time, the Big Player with Limit Orders come into play, which we cannot see properly with the best software. But there is still a way to see the order flow in the right context. I would like to refer to slide 3 again, where we can identify cumulative market orders. If these cumulative market orders were not initiated by a big player, there is only one possible explanation for it. Most of these cumulative market orders are triggered stops, by institutional and retail traders. This provides enough bit and ask so that the big players can fill their limit orders. We know that someone accepts this market order, but the total volume of an iceberg order is still hidden from us. To find out whether the cumulative orders are market orders from a big player or triggered stops, we need 5 important representations. The DOM, the time and sales list, an overview of the cumulative market orders, a heat map and a forex chart where we identify the possible stops.

Let's start with the stop identification and take a closer look at the last trading day on Friday.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The card shows the EURUSD in M5 from 07:00 to 19:00 CET from the last trading day on Friday. The price was in a downward trend to point A and then changed direction. The traders who managed to get into the price relatively early were spared from the first return to point B, but some have already been stopped here. The price reached a new high at point C and prompted many traders to put suit their stops at point B. From point C there was a stronger return to point D. Most short traders were only able to get in the middle of this movement. In the course of the price at point D, many traders who hoped for a long, at point C were stopped. First of all, we notice that price levels A and D are almost identical. It seems like a resistance zone that could not be broken. Added to this, the fact that the price had not formed a new low caused many traders to continue betting on a long trade. With the move to point F, these long traders were removed from the market. After, the price went to point G, trying to stop the short traders or reduce their profits. The price movements to point H were again a masterpiece of the stop hunting strategy. Point I clearly shows again that this zone is a strong resistance zone that cannot be broken. The course of zone J has also tried to catapult the last long traders out of the market.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Let us now consider the course of the euro FX in a slightly different way. This is a heat map, in combination with cumulative and non-cumulative market orders. A heat map is suitable for making liquidity changes from the Dom visible in the chat. The minimum and maximum liquidity can be individually filtered to make it easier to identify larger limits. If the volume is above the minimum or maximum volume, the price level is shown in proportion to the volume. In connection with the cluster search, you can, for example, filter how much of the touched limit orders were actually executed, in order to identify fake orders. I decided not to do this now, because we will go into more detail in our project 10.

At point A we see green lines that show the liquidity of the buy limit orders in this overview. The red lines at point B show the liquidity of the sell limit orders. The green circles at point C show the cumulative buy market orders and the green triangles are the cumulative buy market orders. At point D we see a large red circle, which represents an accumulated sell market orders, a red triangle is an unaccumulated sell market orders. In this overview of 12 hours in a 1 second chart, you can of course not exactly recognize the individual liquidity, so we zoom in a little closer to see the presentation a little better.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

First of all we see how the price is pushed down a little more and at point A the triggered stops are absorbed by the liquidity. At point B we see that there is still strong liquidity in the market. In principle, this is a safeguard for the big players because they do not know exactly how many stops there are in the market. When stops are triggered, a kind of chain reaction occurs, with each stop (sell market orders) pushing the price further down.

This liquidity that we see here in the market should absorb further stops in an emergency. We can clearly see that even the big players cannot always accurately assess a market. After that, the market went up again and we can already see that liquidity is building up early to intercept the buy market orders (short trader stops) at point C. At point D, too, there was increased liquidity in the buy limit area, which ultimately pushed the price up.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

First of all, at point A we see a strong zone in the area of liquidity in order to intercept possible stops of the short traders. At Point B, we see buy limit orders absorb the market sell orders, but this may have been a partial sale in dollars. However, this situation did not justify a strong upward price trend. At point C there were further exits from the dollar but no typical absorption to buy the euro. Finally, a very strong absorption took place at point D, the strong liquidity at point E was an additional security to absorb further bid. The price then went up and we see at Point F that the big players are absorbing the stops of the short traders and pushing the price up. In addition, some cumulative buy market orders also came in. From point G, there is greater liquidity on the sell limit side to realize partial sales. Between points G and H, more buyers enter the market, while the big players partially hold their positions. There was no clear indication of a stronger decline.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

At Point A we see how the big players with strong sell limit orders buy into the stops of the short traders. The price initially runs down to Point B. We first recognize that the stops of the long traders are triggered, but very little of it is absorbed by the big players. For me that was a clear indication that the price could continue to go down. Of course there was a little stop run again and then the course was pushed down. Let us first look at point D, there was a lot of absorption and the zone had already been defined 15 minutes beforehand. The course jumped down a bit due to the stop run, but was well intercepted by the big players. First the price was pushed up again and there was another small stop run to point F. There we can clearly see that a large player with strong market orders came into the market. At the same time, there was a strong resistance zone in the form of strong liquidity on the sell limit side. This should show retail traders that the upward price will not get through. Many traders fell for it and entered into a short trade. When the course got to the strong limit orders, it was deleted and the course was pushed up sharply. The stops of the short traders (market ask) led to further upward movements.

Conclusion:

In combination with the Cluster Search, the heat map is ideal for finding out what is currently happening in the market. In addition, the DOM, the time and sales list, an overview of the cumulative market orders and a stop identification should be used. Of course, this approach is not a holy grail either, but in combination with the other information, you can already work out a small market advantage. Another interesting aspect is a kind of swing trading, where you trade with the big players from stop to stop. In the heat map you can see how strong these stops are in individual cases. This procedure is particularly interesting if you can identify the stops of the individual traders beforehand. And the Forex Chart is very suitable for this stop identification. I hope that with this detailed contribution I was able to describe Project Nos. 9 and 10 in a little more detail. First of all, it is important to familiarize yourself with stophunting in our project No. 9. As soon as we have extensive experience in this area, Project 10 will focus on what exactly happens in the market if these stops are caught. The big players will always run in zigzag lines from stop to stop to get the necessary liquidity. Those who are able to identify these stops beforehand can achieve significantly better profits in the Forex market without future data. That is the first step we will take.

--- 帖子 #1289 ---
Crucial market analysis

[quote=baxter01;12727589]@Bionics Hello Michael, I´m far away from having that much of expeience than you have. I`ve read most of your inside views on the market. Please allow me to ask if I understood most things ok.

Hello baxter01,

I warmly welcome you to us and I am pleased that this blog is of interest to you. My many years of experience are based solely on my own assumptions and are very likely not to represent the market as it actually is. Therefore, I can only answer your questions within the framework of my views, which may differ from other opinions. Every opinion about the market has its justification, because even a watch that has stopped shows the correct time twice a day. The aim of every retailer is to be able to read the right time on this watch as often as possible. I would like to comment on your questions.

1. Market movements are almost driven by the interest of the BIG players. So ... we should try to follow the money. (I'm having trouble seeing what they're up to.)

85% of the Forex market turnover is generated by 12 banks, so it is imperative that these big players move the market in their favor. It is therefore perfectly understandable that institutional traders and retail traders are trying to follow these movements. However, this is a very big challenge, since most of the big players' entries and exits occur through limit orders that cannot be identified in the market. These are the well-known iceberg orders, which are used to a large extent to hide the true intentions. To fill their limit orders, the big players need a large amount of market orders. The big players find the largest number of market orders in the area of stops, since these stops are usually at similar price levels. Of course, a distinction must be made between scalper, day trader and swing trader. The big players also work with market orders to push the price in their desired direction or trigger stops. If the stops of other market participants are caught, stops trigger a chain reaction first and the price moves strongly up or down. The big players either use this movement to steer the price in their direction or they absorb these stops (market orders) with their limit orders. The key is to always see this approach in the right context of the market and that is indeed the biggest challenge. This contribution will help you.

Liquidity versus volume

2. There is no real support / resistance or supply / demand that we can rely on.

Basically, you have to know that the big players themselves do not consider any resistance zones because they create them themselves. If a price goes down and bounces two or three times at a certain resistance zone, the retail trader is signaled that this is a strong zone that cannot be broken. Many assume, that the big players in this zone have absorbed market orders in order to push the price up sharply. This causes many traders to build a long position (ask). This ask is now absorbed by the big players unnoticed and they push the price down. This triggers the stops of the long traders, creating a chain reaction and breaking the fake resistance zone. Most traders are out of the market and are now betting on a short position. These short positions are used by the big players to get out of their positions.

More sellers enter the market and the price continues to fall. In this phase, the big player starts collecting ask again and then pushes the price up. If the big players were unable to collect enough ask or bid, an equilibrium is created first. Within this equilibrium, the big player is as tame as a lion who has just eaten a gazelle. The course is driven back and forth within a range to collect ask or bid in peace. To trade this range successfully, you should be a scalper and get out of your position relatively quickly in order to trade the range. Since I have not worked earlier with future data before, this was a successful approach for me.

3. There is no overbought / oversold product on the market.

For example, the RSI is a standard indicator that was developed back in the 1970s. For the selected time horizon within different periods, the sum of the period rate winners and the period rate losses is calculated. The two sums are then compared to each other and thus measure the inner strength of a trend compared to itself. Values above 70 are classified as overbought and values below 30 are classified as oversold. This oscillator is calculated from the price. The price is solely the result of liquidity, volume and time. This is a crucial point that is very important. This is proof that the price has nothing to do with the value of a currency. The problem in the Forex market is that we don't get volume and liquidity data there. How do you want to be able to calculate volume and liquidity solely from the price? When I work with a price indicator, I deal with the effect without knowing the cause. In addition, a price indicator is always lagging behind the price itself. A lot of back tests have been carried out with the RSI, although the profit rates were not convincing due to the spreads and broker costs. Since the market is not based on price, but only on volume and liquidity, there can be no overbought or oversold for me. But that's just my opinion.

4. Without sufficient volume, there are no reliable price movements.

The market consists of only two factors. This is liquidity in the form of limit orders and bid and ask in the form of market orders. Both factors are needed to cause a market movement. A market order can only enter the market if there is liquidity in the form of a limit order. I described detailed examples in my blog.

Identification of the big players

The wrong truth?

5. Known patterns / candle formations are also seen and used by the big players to "chase" our money.

First of all, candle patterns like the Doji are a pure coincidence of the times. You can see this at the latest when you work with a tick chart. As soon as you change a few ticks, the doji suddenly disappears. It is the same with candle formations. The big players only run from stop to stop to collect their necessary bid and ask. This creates candle patterns or candle formations that big players like to use to mislead traders. In addition to the RSI, MACD, Fibonacci, the 200 EMA is also often used by the big players, as many traders orientate themselves to it.

You write that many retailers have wrong thoughts, but this is primarily because the industry and brokers, with their indicators, have just started these wrong thoughts. The retailer is not at fault here. Both the big players and many brokers win if we lose, so why should you tell the truth to retailers when an entire industry lives on it. It's the same as in the medical field. I am convinced that we could have put a cancer drug on the market long ago, but the industry is making billions from chemotherapy, why should they change it?  It will only change when the pressure on the industry becomes so great that it has to move.

That a very good money management in the Forex market decides about long-term success is absolutely correct. You can find some good examples in my blog.

Easy increase in trading efficiency!

You write that you have problems creating a system from all this information. Unfortunately, I have to tell you that there will never be a long-term profitable system. This is simply because the limit orders of the big players are invisible. And that is exactly the decisive factor. How do you want to build a system with information that is not available at all? Here the human being has an advantage over the machine with his feelings. Based on his experience, he is able to cancel his trade immediately while the machine is running in the stop loss. Of course, the big players can be supported in the form of algorithms to bring the necessary limit orders or market orders to the market. They can also be given information about when the highest probability of winning can be expected. But the main decisions are still made by people. That is why billions are invested in analysts, market observers and traders. It is like in Formula 1 racing, you can build the best Formula 1 cars, but in the end the racer decides whether to succeed or not.

Many traders have a habit of closing a trade too soon or leaving it in the red for too long. However, this can be optimized with years of training. Trading is a profession like a doctor, notary or lawyer, that's why you can earn so much. However, you also need a lot of time to study and experience in practice. Time is a decisive factor here, which unfortunately can only be shortened with the right knowledge.

And that's exactly what we want to advance in this blog. A crucial point is the Stophunting, which we are currently dealing with. Perhaps these ideas and insights can provide you with interesting aspects. If the information helps you, read this blog. Any idea you get can help you move forward.

Michael Jordan was once asked why he enjoys defending the ball so well? Thereon he replied, that he cannot play basketball, when the other has the ball. Maybe we also have to develop such a passion for our profession.

I wish you all the best and I would be happy if this blog can help you in the future.

Lovely wishes

Michael

Follow Smart Money !!!

Stoprun, Stophunting, Stopfishing

Hello dear subscribers,

85% of turnover in the Forex market is generated by 12 banks, so it is essential that these big players move the market in their favor. It is also perfectly understandable that retail traders are trying to follow these big players. This is a big challenge at first, but it can be achieved with the right strategy. We'll see some examples of this today. In order to follow a big player, you first have to know exactly how it works and what happens. First of all, the way big players work differs from retail traders in almost all areas.

Let's take a closer look at the differences:

Big players move the market because they often work with a few hundred thousand lots in Forex. Retail traders can rarely move the price in Forex (EURUSD) by 1/10 pip, since an average of approximately 1,200 lots are required for this.

Retail traders can enter and exit the market immediately. Since the big players work with very large positions, they are unable to bring their positions directly into the market. You are forced to look for a suitable volume. For this reason, the big players rely on collecting ask or bid in the sideways phases that is made available by a wide variety of market participants. In an accumulation phase, Ask is collected to push the price up in the medium term, while in the distribution phase bid is collected to push the price down in the medium term. Therefore, a trader should always analyze what happens within an equilibrium.

Market orders are transactions that should be executed as quickly as possible at the current market price, a limit order specifies the maximum or minimum price at which you want to buy or sell. Most retail traders work with market orders for their entries and exits, while the big players execute their entries and exits almost exclusively with limit orders, so they usually get the best price.

Most retail traders work with stops, while the big players do without them or at most work with hedge strategies.

Big players often let their big positions run up to 50 pip down before they push the price up or down again. Most retail traders are already in the stop loss.

Big players buy in a falling market and sell in a rising market. The retail trader buys in rising markets and sells in falling markets.

Retail traders are guided by resistance zones that are initiated by the big players.

The price arises from the volume, liquidity and time. Big players work with volume and liquidity, while the retail trader works with price and time.

Retail traders work with indicators to make a profit, the big players only work with indicators to see where you can take the most money from the retail trader.

Big players are more like day traders or swing traders and focus on the medium-term area, while many retail traders are more short-term oriented.

Big players have a professional technique with special algorithms, employ top analysts, traders and mainly deal with outside money. Retail traders own a PC with a mediocre internet connection and often trade with money that they need to live.

Retail traders are looking for inside information, big players are the insider because they know exactly what will happen next. It is not rumors, news or meetings that determine the market, but exclusively the strategies of the big players.

These are the major differences between big players and retail traders. You can only face an opponent if you know his weaknesses exactly. Than we can take a advantage of this. What is the biggest weakness of big players?

The big players are not able to bring their positions directly into the market, they are forced to collect large volumes in sideways phases (equilibrium). Since most of the big players' entries and exits occur through limit orders, they need market orders. This means that the big players primarily need as many market orders as possible at one price level. And where can you find them? Answer: In triggered stops. That is exactly why the big players concentrate on Stophunting. There, large quantities of market orders are released within seconds, which you only have to collect. And it is exactly this collection that takes place in secret, so that most market participants do not even realize what is happening there. These are the well-known iceberg orders that are used so that no big price jumps occur and to hide the true intentions.

If the stops of the other market participants are caught, the stops first trigger a chain reaction and the price moves strongly up or down. The big players either use this movement to steer the price in their direction or they absorb these stops (market orders) with their limit orders. In addition, the unpleasant market participants are removed from the market, which could disrupt the actual price development. The key is to always see this approach in the right context of the market and that is indeed the biggest challenge.

About 15% of the total turnover in the Forex market is secured with stops, which are almost exclusively institutional and retail traders. In the order book you can see the market order and the limit order, but not the stops and it is exactly these stops that exert a magical attraction on the big players. What many do not even know, this stophunting takes place permanently in the market. In principle, this is not bad will on the part of the big players when they shoot market players out of the market.

The big players are always looking for liquidity. The $ 400 million the big players earn every day is largely the result of stophunting. In addition to scalpers, there are also day traders and swing traders up to the very long-term position traders. It is clear that we have to start from different stop sizes. For this reason, it is important to recognize where the individual stops of the traders are. As soon as you identify these stops, you can use it to estimate a further course of the course. With pure Forex data, it is theoretically possible to improve the probability of winning on the basis of identified stops.

First and foremost, a price always consists of Zigzag patterns because the big players need the necessary market orders for their liquidity. Therefore, the identification of the stops is a crucial key point in this market segment. We have to keep in mind that retail traders are following stops, making it easier for big players to achieve this liquidity (stops) faster with a counter trend.

Absorption via passive liquidity creates resistance zones that the big players never pay attention to because you create them yourself. If a price goes down and bounces two or three times at a certain resistance zone, the retail trader is signaled that this is a strong zone that cannot be broken. Most support and resistance zones have been initiated, so you always have to ask yourself why the big player created this zone.

A big advantage for the big players is the fact that retail traders follow trends, even though there are actually no trends. A trend is described as a particularly profound and sustainable course development. For me, a trend is just a price trend that can develop in the opposite direction at any time. You can discuss trends forever, and there will always be different views. An upward trend is identified if ever higher highs and higher lows are formed in the price trend. Downward trends are identified when steadily falling lows and constantly falling highs are formed in the price trend. Big players know these rules very well and use them to obtain the necessary volume. In order to study this procedure in more detail, we first work with 3 auxiliary indicators, which you can find here with a template for the MT4.

Supporting indicators for Project No.9

Let's start with my interpretation of a course in the EURUSD M15. I would like to note that this is an interpretation. Interpretation (Latin interpretatio "interpretation, translation, explanation") means in the general sense the understanding or the subjectively regarded as plausible interpretation of something given or at least something existing. This is only my view of the market, so I do not claim that my assessment is correct in all respects. In addition, misunderstandings may arise due to the translation.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Point A

Initially, the price in the M15 went down sharply. The candles are displayed in the form of a dark gray bar chart, however in our example the bar charts cannot be recognized. Within the bar charts, I am only interested in the particularly strong candles. If a new trend suddenly arises from a strong movement, it is quite unlikely that many traders have trade into it. Therefore, there are no or few stops below or above these strong bar charts.

Point B

Since the price has been going down for a while, the liquidity in the buy limit orders decreases. This is also completely logical, since many traders are short-oriented and tend to bring sell limit orders or sell market orders to the market. If the big player tried to push the price further down, a lack of liquidity in the buy limit orders leads to a limit. Therefore, there is a high level of liquidity in the sell limit orders at the time. The Big Player purchases shortly before point B because there is enough bid. From point B, he pushes the price up with strong buy market orders. Other participants who believe in a long, also join.

Point C

At point C, the stops of traders who still believed in a short at point B were triggered. These triggered stops are buy market orders, which the big player absorbs with sell limit orders. This gives the big player an even better short entry and pushes the price down again.

Point D

On the way from point C to point D, the stops of the long traders who got in near point B, are triggered and initially accelerate the price further down. When the price reached point D, the liquidity in the sell limit orders was again significantly higher than in the buy limit orders. For this reason, the price was pushed up again.

Point E

First of all, we notice a number of 105 that was reached at the top of Point E. This number is the average pip / 10 each candle has reached between points D and E. This value is higher than most values. First of all, this is an indication that the upward trend in the price has been strong and can possibly be identified as a pullback. In addition, it can be a sign that the price is slowly preparing for an upward trend.

Point F

After the pullback to point E, the course first runs to point F, where it reaches the lowest point. With a value of 40.2, it was an above-average trend that could continue in a medium period.

Point G

At first it looked as if it could be a pullback and many suspected that the downward trend was not yet complete. In the price trend at point H, the long traders from point G were stopped first. Already here you could see with future data that the big players absorbed this ask and did not use it to accelerate the price down. This already gave an indication that the price would no longer go down.

Point H

At Point H, many traders thought that the price was now going down and put more short positions in the market. These shorts were absorbed and the course pushed up. When the point H had not formed a new low compared to the point F and was slowly rising again, some traders went long.

Point I

The price was pushed to Point I above average, but no new high was formed. For some traders, this was a sign that the price would go lower, so they took a short position at Point I.

Point J

The return to Point J was weak above average. This was not a problem for long traders who started at point H, as their stops were below point H. At Point J, other short traders have entered the market.

Point K

At Point K, the price compared to Point I is build a new high. This was initiated by the big players so that the long traders from Point H could pull their stops to Point J. This ensured that there was sufficient liquidity available for price pressure downwards.

Point L

Shortly after the price at Point K hit a new high, there were many long traders hoping for a further upward trend. First, their stops were used to let the price run down. The long traders' stops below Point J were absorbed to collect further ask. We can see that the move to Point L was an above average weak movement. This initially spoke for a future, stronger upward trend. What is striking is that the stops that were under Point H and Point F were not picked up. Initially, this was not necessary as there weren't many traders there, and it took a few more stops to push the price down further in the long run. It is interesting to see that Point H and Point L showed an allegedly strong resistance zone that could not be broken at first glance. Here some traders were initially undecided and waited for a while.

Point M

The course of the course at point M initially stopped the short traders who had their stops above points G, I and K. Point M was a new high that brought many long traders into the market. They were stopped again when returning to Point N.

Point N

The long traders who entered the market from Point L had their stops below Point L and were waiting for another trend upwards.

Point O

The upward course of the price was above average and stopped approximately at the level of point M. Here a strong resistance zone was created, which could not be broken upwards. In addition, the short traders were not stopped via Point M because their volume was still needed.

Point P

The return to Point P was a smart move, initially an obvious upward trend was created because no new low was formed and the long traders from Point N were spared. This brought further long traders into the market that are betting on an upward trend.

Point Q

First, the short traders of Point M and O were stopped, which gave the big player enough volume in the bid. After another high was formed with Point Q, further long traders came onto the market. The big players used the stops of these long traders for the first sharp drop in prices to Point R.

Point R

The stops of the long traders at Point Q initially pushed the price down. The long traders' stops at Point N and P helped increase the downward pressure. In the end the stops of the long traders under point L, H and F were picked up. With the Point R, a new low was formed against Point F. Many were now convinced that the course would continue to go down.

Point S

The short traders from Point R gave the necessary volume to reach Point S. This was again an above-average strong pullback upwards.

Point T

Another smart move by the big players, no new low was formed and the suspicion arose that it could be another upward trend.

Point U

On the way to Point U there were again some long traders who gave the big players the volume they needed to push the price further down. The short traders who started at Point S were not triggered.

Point V

In the course of the course towards Point V, the long traders of Point R and T were initially removed from the game. This was an above-average downward trend. Against point R and T a new low was formed and was the reason for many traders to put on a short.

Point W

There was initially a pullback to Point W, whereby the short traders from Point S and U were spared.

Point X

Here the stops of the long traders from point V were triggered. Based on the above-average strong downward movement, you can see that the big players have worked with strong market orders. Some short traders who started at Point S and U moved their stops to Point W. Point X was another low compared to Point V, which brought further short traders onto the market. These short traders were absorbed by the big players to push the price up again.

Point Y

Now a new high against point W was formed, but was not yet a confirmed upward trend. The stops at Point W have been picked up. Many thought it could go lower and took short positions.

Point Z

First, the course ran down a little to Point Z. Why didn't the course go further  down? There were no more stops to be expected. From point X to point Y, the first candle was a strong movement that ran to the height of point Z. Few people expected this movement and therefore there were few long traders. So there was no interest from the big players to push the price further down because there were few stops from long traders to be expected. More ask was absorbed and collected in the movements from point R to point Z, so one could expect a further upward trend. In addition, there were more short traders in the market at the time and if a big player has collected enough ask, he tries to push the price up. The stops of the short traders help him. As soon as these stops are triggered, you immediately release Ask, which pushes the price up.

Point 1

The big players use this fact to bring the course to Point 1. At Point S, U, W and Y there were still enough stops from the short traders that were used for this upward swing. We now want to take a closer look at this upward trend.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The first candle that was created between the points X and Y was very strong, which nobody expected (red arrow). That was the reason why the pullback to Point Z didn't go any further down. Since very few had expected the strong red movement, there also have been few stops. The prospect of further Ask would have been relatively small. The pullback from point Y to Z had only one goal. They wanted to pull the long traders who got inside the strong red candle out of circulation. This ensured that there were hardly any long traders in the game.

The first candle in the movement from point Z to point 1 was again very strong. After some long traders had already been taken out of the game in the movement from point y to z, many were not sure whether it was actually going up. After the yellow candle crossed Point Y, many considered it to be a confirmed upward trend. Most of them only entered the market above Point Y, so there was little chance that there would be many stops below Point Y. From point 1 to point 2 there was initially a small pullback, which gave hope to the remaining long traders. Now the Big Playen use a well-known trick. With point 3 a new high was formed, which caused many long traders to pull their stops to point 2. Some short traders that had set a downward trend at Point 1 were also stopped.

With the move from Point 3 to Point 4, further long traders were withdrawn from the market. Here you can clearly see that the big players under Point 4 did not expect any further stops. At Point 4, many believed that the price was now going down and took a short position.

We now have the following situation, the big players are in the market with their ask positions and are already in the plus. How do they get out of their position best? Answer: By finding as much bid as possible in the form of stops. And for this you need the stops of the short traders. Let's take a closer look at the situation There was a long downward trend from point 1 to point 2 and from point 3 to point 4. During this time, a large number of traders positioned themselves short, placing their stops above points 1 or 3. The big players could therefore assume that enough stopps are available via points 1 and 3 to push the price up sharply and at the same time get out of their positions. The strong green candle clearly shows that the stops of the short traders were picked up from points 1 and 3.

At point 5, a strong resistance zone developed because the course ran twice to this zone. Many short traders have entered the market there. The pullback to Point 6 ended in the area where the big players no longer expected further stops. And this zone ends within the strong green candle.

Most big players have left their euro positions in the course of the green candle and have already started buying the dollar. When the course to Point 6 was over, the big players got the necessary Ask, to push the course up again. There the short trader stops from point 5 and the blue arrow were triggered and bid was absorbed in the blue candle. Then the price went down.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

If we ask ourselves why the course went down again from point 7, the answer is relatively simple. When the price reached Point 7, there was no short-term stop liquidity that was worth collecting. This is also evident from the green lines in the chart, which show the possible stops of the short traders or where there is enough bid. In the lower area there was strong liquidity in the ask, so the big players were able to get out of their dollar positions and at the same time buy the euro and then push the price up again.

So we can see that the course is not random, but is always the result where the big players find the most liquidity in the form of stops. However, it is always a question of whether you use the stops to push the price up or down, or whether you absorb the stops. This essentially decides on the further price of the course. We have found, that the market does not provide the big player, with infinite volumes and therefore they have to collect them. We can take advantage of this weak point of the big players by trying to find out where the next volume point is that they are approaching. This could help many retail traders to make their decisions a little more concrete in the future and make more profit at the same time. One could also participate in the big player's stop chase and earn money when the colleagues are stopped. Although this is not collegial but due to the anonymity in the market, nobody notices that. In my eyes, the procedure of stop identification is the only way to trade price data in the forex market a little more successfully. However, the crucial data is missing on what the big players do with the triggered stops. And we only get this information with the future data.

First of all, I recommend that you look at the market from the perspective of the stops and differentiate between long and short traders. There will give you crucial information that will take you further.

I wish you a successful trading week

best regards
