Project No. 10

A completely new market view

Hello dear subscribers,

As promised, we are starting today with our new project No. 10. In this project we will see that the limit orders are more crucial for the long-term price trend than the market orders. And I will show you how to make limit orders visible. In the next few weeks we will deal with the future data in more detail. Our project no. 9 (Stophunting) will continue to accompany us. If you want to be successful in this market in the long term, you need to take a closer look,  how big players work. A price does not change because a moving average has crossed, an RSI is overbought or a fibozone has been reached, but because there are more short traders than long traders in a downward movement and more long traders than short traders in an upward movement. The big players determine the market and they pursue a goal. This goal can only be recognized if you know what they are up to. Their plan can be identified by the limit orders. We want to start with that today.

In the past 10 years I was lucky enough to take the smaller movements up to 10 pip within one equilibrium and was therefore able to act profitably. However, I was unlucky enough to never know exactly what was happening in the market. FF motivated me to write down my thoughts on trading over 2 years ago. At first I tried to describe my approach exactly and quickly realized that this is not so easy. The more I wrote, the more questions I had. Every question I answered myself took me a step further, but more and more questions came up and prompted me to dig deeper into the subject. With the tick charts, a kind of breakthrough came into the world of stock market data. At first I wanted to know exactly how these tick charts are calculated in Forex and at the same time I recognized the incompleteness and limitation of this calculation. Many years ago I heard about the volume that was presented with footprint charts, volume profile and market profile. But all these chart representations make no sense in Forex, since no data feeds are provided for them. Why deal with something that is not feasible.

First of all, I wanted to know how a tick chart in Forex differs from a tick chart in Future. So I got futures data, but these pure futures data alone couldn't give me a clear answer. The MT5 was the worst alternative to optimally display futures data, as well as other trading platforms such as Ninja Trader, Multicharts, Sierra Chart or Jigsaw could not satisfy my requirements. I chose a professional proprietary trading platform. This enabled me to filter and display the pure stock market data in such a way that it made sense to me. I started to compare the tickchart in the forex with the tickchart in the future. It struck me that the course behaved almost exactly the same, but the prices were different due to the swaps. I am one of the 4% of professional Forex traders in Europe who can trade up to 400 with a lever and at the same time I have extremely good protection in the event of an uncontrolled breakout. Since the EURUSD has the highest liquidity in the Forex market with over $ 2 trillion in daily turnover and at the same time has the least drawdowns, I wanted to continue trading in the Forex market.

So I tried to find another way. I started organizing my forex trading based only on the futures data. Initially, this was a very daring version, especially since it was a matter of two different markets. It didn't work so well at first because I didn't pay attention to some things. However, it was an alternative that gave me the motivation to take a closer look at the volume. A big aspect benefited me. For years I have been dealing intensively with the approach of big players and high-frequency traders. If you want to be really successful in this market, you cannot avoid it. I started to deal more intensively with the footprint chart, volume chart and market profile. That didn't get me anywhere. The next step was the DOM and the Times and Sales list. This information was much more accurate, but I was still on the wrong track. I returned to the big players' way of working and started to deal with them in more detail. The big players move the market, that is undisputed, but how do they move the market? Let's start with that.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

At point A the sell market orders come into the market, which meet the buy limit orders at point B. At point C the buy market orders come into the market that meet the sell limit orders point D. At Point E we see the monthly volume of buy market orders and at Point F the monthly volume of sell market orders. Point G shows the price, the daily volume and the number of trades at the respective price level. You can add other ads to this DOM, such as spoofing, which shows added or deleted limit orders. For our example, I did without it. The market orders eat their way into the limit orders and as soon as the liquidity is used up, it goes to the next price level. If many market orders come in, but the price does not change, the market orders are held up by the limit orders. This means that more and more limit orders are added at this price level, one speaks of an absorption.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

A footprint chart is a concrete representation of the DOM in the area of market orders. The time frame is specified by the dealer. At Point A we see such a footprint representation. The ask or the market buy orders are on the right, the bid or the market sell orders are on the left. The white frame indicates the highest volume in the candle. 726 lots were traded on the ask side, while 85 lots were traded on the bid side.

At Point B, a beginner's first question comes to mind: how can it be that 125 lot market buy and only 0 lot market sell were traded at one price level? First of all, we need to know that the market buy orders and market sell orders can never meet eachother. The market sell orders meet the limit buy orders and the brand buy orders meet the limit sell orders. Therefore, a footprint chart is a bit confusing at first, because the market buy orders and market sell orders stand side by side. It is just a representation of how much lot was traded at a price level. The red and green numbers each show an imbalance of the individual market orders. Although this is an interesting note,  I would not make any trading decisions with it.

At Point C we see the total volume that was traded at the upper price level. This is a total of 1766 lots. 1610 lots were traded in ask and 156 lots in bid. Ask minus Bid is delta, in our case a positive delta of 1454 Lot. These are exclusively market orders. So we can initially state that only the market orders are able to move the market, while the limit orders are able to stop the market. Since the big players move the market, one could conclude that the big players primarily deal with market orders. However, this is a false assumption, which I will discuss in more detail. The vast majority of price representations primarily refer to market orders, only in the DOM and in the heat map can limit orders be displayed at first glance.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

As we have already established, the big players are not able to immediately get large orders in the market and then push the price in their direction. Therefore, they are sometimes forced to collect Ask or Bid over several days within certain price levels and then push the price towards them. For me, these are the so-called equilibrium phases, which are shown here with accumulation and distribution. During these phases, the big players have the task of collecting ask or bid and at the same time always keeping the price within this range. Before the breakout, you have to stop potential followers to avoid being delayed in your breakout.

The big question now is how a big player can best collect within an accumulation or distribution phase without most market participants noticing. We know that market orders are visible in the market, while limit orders cannot be identified. For this reason, iceberg orders are primarily used for these collection campaigns. Iceberg orders are nothing more than limit orders, which are controlled by algorithms and absorb market orders at certain price levels. We should know that absorption does not take place at one price level, but always at several.

Let's imagine a big player wants to push a price down, which means we are in a distribution phase. To do this, he first has to collect bids, so in the area of sell limit orders the algorithms are instructed to buy a certain number of market buy orders without giving themselves away. This means big players have to be careful not to absorb too much at one level, otherwise the market could quickly realize that this is a strong resistance level and many traders would take long positions. When a big player collects limit orders within an equilibrium, it is a lot of work at first. The price has to be kept within the range, stops have to be started because there is immediate volume available and if enough has been collected, a suitable time has to be selected at which the volatility may be somewhat higher.

In these actions, the employed traders of the big players must work together, to work towards a common goal. Different traders get the order to collect a predetermined number of limit orders at different price levels using different algorithms. As soon as they have completed their collection campaign and have initially pushed the course in an opposite direction to trigger the stops of the followers, the algorithms begin to push the course upwards. This takes the form of cumulative small market orders that the market initially does not notice. I have observed these algorithms in the last few months and it is relatively easy to read them. We will deal with this in more detail, however. Stophunting is also a crucial factor for big players. Possible stops are easiest to identify in the Forex market, since we have 5 times more accurate price positions there than in the Future market.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

First of all, I divided the big players and retail traders according to supply and demand. The demand comes within an accumulation phase and the supply within a distribution phase. Let us first consider how the individual market participants behave in the individual phases.

Within an accumulation phase, a big player needs Ask, which he tries to collect with limit buy orders. For this he has to buy the euro and it is a passive order, as this does not move the market. Within an accumulation phase there is a so-called range in which the big player collects ask. As soon as the price moves extremely out of this range, the big player is forced to push the price back into this range. At the low of this range, he has to buy the euro with buy market orders in order to push the price up again. At the high of this range, he has to buy the dollar to push the price down again.

Once he has collected enough, the crucial question is whether the majority of the participants are short or long in the market. If many participants have taken a long position, there will be a stophunting. To do this, the big player must first buy the dollar heavily in order to push the price down. On the way down, the long trader's first stops begin to burst. He has to intercept these stops with buy limit orders. As soon as he suspects no further stops, he starts selling the dollar. This sale releases a high number of ask and pushes the price up. In addition, it will push the price up in the form of cumulative market buy orders. The price  upwards in zigzags, the background to this is that the big player needs new volume again and again to bring the price up further. For this he uses the stops of the retail traders.

Because the price continues to rise, there are more and more retail traders joining a long trade. As soon as the volume has reached a corresponding size, the big player begins to exit the euro with limit sell orders. Since this is done with limit orders, most market participants do not notice that the big player is already getting out. If the price does not reach the limit orders of the big players, they can of course also exit the market with markets sell orders. However, this is perceived by the market and could immediately trigger a turnaround. Then the big player would have problems getting out of his position. During the distribution phase, the opposite is true, as you can see on the table.

Since a retail trader can enter the market directly but does not move the price, his trading activities are also restricted accordingly. In most cases, beginners focus exclusively on market orders for entry and exit, with a take profit belonging to the category of limit orders. As soon as a retail trader is stopped, a respective market order is released. In order for the big players to intercept these stops, they are forced to place limit orders in the market.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Here I have now compared the big players and the retail traders in the accumulation and distribution phase. If a big player wants to collect ask in an accumulation phase, he has to buy the euro. In return, he needs a retail trader who either buys the dollar or sells the euro. With its buy limit orders, the big player intercepts the market orders of the retail traders. In order to understand the market context exactly, I recommend that you first deal with these two tables in detail. It is also important to recognize in the market whether a big player is currently buying the dollar or selling the euro. In both cases, Bid come in the market, but there is a crucial difference.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

In the picture we see two volume profiles from two different days in the Euro FX. The volume is the addition of bid and ask. There are many trainers who swear by this volume profile and use it to make concrete trading decisions. For me, this is only a representation to determine in which price ranges a stronger struggle between the different market participants has taken place. Deriving specific resistance zones for the future from this is more realistic than an RSI or MACD, but the decisive factor for me is who won in the individual price ranges. And this cannot be clearly determined in a volume profile. Of course, one could now say that the market tried to keep the price high and then failed and therefore the price went down. In my opinion, however, this is a vague statement that can usually only be made once the course has already been completed. As I said, this view is interesting to determine, in which area an increased volume took place, but not more.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

In this picture we now see a delta of market orders. As we know, the delta is the result of ask and bid. If we see a green bar, more ask than bid was traded on the price level, if we see a red bar, more bid than ask was traded on the price level. If we only looked at the day candle at Point A and had to make a decision about where the price would go next, many would assume that the price would tend to go up. At point B, the price went down and we see that a lot of Ask was traded on the lower three levels. This could be an indication, that the price will now up again. The opposite was the case, however, because the price after go down sharply. So we find that the market orders that move the market do not appear to be an indicator of a long-term price trend.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Let us briefly recall our first slide, the DOM. If we launch a 1 Lot Sell Market Order and it is activated, a 1 Lot buy limit order must be activated at the same time. We now have a buyer and a seller in the market. First of all, it should not be relevant whether the euro was bought or sold or whether the dollar was bought or sold. When a market buy order comes into the market, a sell limit order has to be activated at the same time. This means that a buyer can only meet one seller. If the market is just starting and a market buy order triggers a sell limit order, it means that both a buyer and a seller are in the market at that moment. And this is exactly the point that gave me the idea.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

If a market buy order simultaneously triggers a limit sell order and a market sell order simultaneously a limit buy order, it is automatically possible to display the limit orders in the market. First you just have to swap the colors. So if a market buy order that is green meets a limit sell order that is red, I just have to swap the colors of Bid and Ask to make the limit order visible.

With this in mind, let's take another look at the first day candle at Point A. We now see a strong delta in the sell limit area. One could conclude from this that the price continues to fall. Also in the second day candle in the upper area, a stronger sell limit delta was created, which pushed the price down. A stronger sell limit delta was also created in the lower area of this day candle, which could justify a further price slide downwards. We have already noticed that while market orders move the market, limit orders determine where the market will go in the long term. With this approach, we have already taken a small step forward, but in principle no rule can be created from it that always applies 100%. The consideration of limit orders is always a long-term one, in addition one must also consider the short and medium-term range. For this we need certain tools from the future area, which we will deal later with in more detail.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

In the footprint chat at Point A we see the total volume on the left and on the right the number of trades that were entered into this price range. At Point B we see a volume chart that shows a filtered total volume. At Point C we see a total daily volume divided by bid and ask and at Point D the division of bid and ask within a single candle. In many trainers' seminars, the presentation of market orders is trained in order to make trading decisions. In the short and medium term this may be correct to a certain extent, but the market is primarily determined by the limits order. And exactly these limit orders are ignored.

In my last report, “Own liquidity for the big players”, I talked about two striking points, where the big players have provided themselves with liquidity. Here you can read the articles again.

Own liquidity for the big players

The Big Player bag of tricks

For all forex traders, at this point the price has only reached a resistance zone twice, nothing more. What is decisive, however, is what happened in the market at that moment and this information can only be obtained from the future market. So if you want to have comprehensive information in the future about what is currently happening in the market, you will inevitably have to deal with the future data. This does not mean that you cannot trade profitably with pure Forex data, but the probability is significantly less than with comprehensive information. But even the information from the future market does not help if you do not filter it properly and present it in such a way that it brings a concrete trading advantage. In our project number 10, in addition to the forex data, we will also deal intensively with the future data and combine them with one another. And exactly this combination will bring you a decisive trading advantage.

How to follow big players with Forex data.

Hello dear subscribers,

In my last article: "A completely new market view" I pointed out a new way of looking at things in order to better follow the big players. The big players focus primarily on limit orders, while most of our chart alignments focus exclusively on market orders. With that, it is initially impossible to identify the big players. Here you can find the article:

A completely new market view

This new way of looking at things takes some getting used to and is unfortunately only possible with real stock market data. Nevertheless, there is also a possibility for pure Forex traders to recognize the short-term strategy changes of the big players. I myself also work with a combination of futures and forex data, because in comparison a price change in the futures market triggers five times as many price changes in the forex market. 2 ticks in the future market correspond to 10 pippettes in the forex market. This means that the Forex market has a clear advantage in the area of price changes and changes can be recorded more quickly.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

In EURUSD H4 we see from point A to B that the price has moved down towards the open gap. Then there was an equilibrium of over a week (point C) and then the price went up to point D. Let us now take a closer look at this downward trend, the equilibrium and the upward trend.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

First of all, we see green and red arrows with a number. The numbers show the average pip / 10 of each candle, within an up or down trend. The larger the number, the stronger the pressure up or down. What creates a stronger upward or downward movement? At point 1 we see that in this upward trend each H4 candle has an average of 6.7 pip. Then the course in motion (Point A) ran to Point 2. In this movement, each H4 candle reached an average of 24.7 pip. So this movement was almost 4 times as strong as the previous movement. In the point 0 to point 1 movement, traders were long-oriented. A big player will always take a counter position to realize his winnings. At point A, he pushed the price down and triggered the long trader's stops. When a long trader's stop is triggered, a bid comes into the market, this bid drives the market further down. The large number of 247.5 (at point 2) means that at point 1 most traders were more long-oriented and at the same time on the way down, the stops of these long traders were triggered. We can see in this picture that from the movement A to the movement E, the numbers of the downward trends were significantly larger than the numbers of the upward trends. In this area there were therefore more long-oriented traders than short-oriented traders.

From point 4 to point 5 we see a number of 11.3 pip in the upward movement. This gives an indication that many traders have taken a short position at Point 4, which is why the price was pushed up a little more. First a small equilibrium was created and we can see that a large number of traders have taken a long position at Point 6. Therefore, the course was pushed down more strongly in movement F. The Bionic Zigzag Oscillator (Point G) shows exactly these strong movements. In the downward movement, we can see that the price as a whole was pushed down more than it was pushed up because the majority of traders took a long position in this area. Of course, the retail traders were not permanently in long positions, but most wherever the green arrows were drawn. The big player then pushed the price down and triggered the stops of the long traders.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The course initially ran into the open gap and there was again an equilibrium. At point A there was initially a stronger downward movement, since at point 0 the majority of traders were long-oriented. At Point A, most retail traders thought the price could close the gap. For this reason, the price was pushed up very strongly by the big players to Point B. Then there was another strong downward movement to Point C and then the course went up. In the Bionic oscillator at Point E we can see how strongly traders were oriented short at Point A short.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

In the now easier upward trend, you can see that points A, B and C achieved significantly stronger values than points D, E and F. This clearly shows again that at this point the majority of traders were oriented in the opposite direction. The oscillator at Point G also shows an overall stronger pressure upwards, which clearly proves that at this point most were short-oriented.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Then the course went to Point A, based on the strength we can see that it was a sustainable upward trend. The strong downward movement to Point B clearly shows that the majority of traders at Point A were still long-oriented. With the Bionic Zigzag Oscillator we can see exactly that at point 2, where the yellow arrows can also be seen, the downward trend has turned into an upward trend.

Of course, the display in the H4, is a long-term presentation, with the bionic zigzag indicator we naturally have the option of breaking the display down to the M1 or in a tick chart down to 8 seconds. This enables us to grasp the smaller trend strengths faster.

In fact, the big players intended to keep driving the price into the gap, but this can be seen better in the future market. Let's first take a closer look at the Delta Limit Orders (yellow frame) in the Future Market.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The respective green and red bars in Euro FX show the respective delta of limit orders. First, the price was pushed down sharply on February 13 and we can see on the low that the big players had already collected stronger sell limit orders.

Also on February 14th and 17th, further sell limit orders were collected in a kind of equilibrium. In the yellow box at point A we can see the stronger sell limit orders. On February 18, the price was finally pushed down and on the low the big players started to collect stronger sell limit orders again. February 19 was also dominated by sell limit orders. The yellow box at points B and C clearly shows a high volume in the sell limit area. At this point, I also assumed a further downward trend.

Then on February 20, a situation arose that the big players had not expected. The majority of traders positioned themselves short because the retail traders hoped that the gap would now be closed. So, the big players had to change their strategy. At Point D you can guess that they have given up previously collected positions to the short-willing retail traders and at the same time started to collect Ask with buy limit orders. The strong bullish candle on February 21 could only arise because many short traders were stopped and the big players pushed the price up to bring their buy limit orders to profit. If the big players had pushed the price down on February 20, there would have been too many retail traders and would have significantly reduced the big players' profits. The decision they made was absolutely right. It is precisely for this reason that it is crucial to monitor the limit orders regularly in order to immediately recognize when the market behavior of the big players changes.

On February 18 and 19, the Big Boys collected sell limit orders to push the price down further, and then on February 20 made the decision to exit their position and collect buy limit orders. On February 19, I myself assumed that the price would continue to decline and was somewhat confused on February 20, when suddenly buy limit orders were collected. Big players are chasing retail traders' stops, so sometimes you have to make quick decisions when the overall situation changes. And it is precisely these changes that we have to watch out for and follow.

You can find some reports on this blog.

--- 帖子 #1360 ---
Volume versus liquidity

Hello dear subscribers,

As we already know, the only reason for price changes is that market orders (volume) meet limit orders (liquidity). While the retail traders primarily work with market orders, the big player collect limit orders in accumulation and distribution phases, pushing the price up or down with market orders. As a rule, they exit their positions with limit orders. In addition, in the past few weeks we have seen in EURUSD how they are able to provide liquidity for themselves. If this approach is successful, it would reduce the number of equilibrium in the future. The EURUSD is best used for experiments because it is the most liquid currency pair with over $ 2 trillion in daily sales.

Almost all trading platforms that are able to read future data concentrate on the market orders. First we have to split the market orders of the big players into cumulative and non-cumulative market orders. A non-cumulative market order is, for example, a 50 lot buy market order that is placed on the market. Let us assume that there are 50 lots on the sell limit side. Now the big, non-cumulative 50 lot buy market order of the big player meets the 50 lot sell limit orders from different market participants, eats up the limit orders and jumps to the next price level. The disadvantage of this approach: All market participants can see this large order. Let's stick to the same example. The big player can now use algorithms to split his 50 lot orders into smaller orders, 5 times 1, 2, 3, and 4 lots. This now creates a cumulative buy market order, which also eats into the sell limit orders and increases the price by one level. However, it now looks as if 20 different market participants are responsible for these orders and not a big player.

Only if the trading software can divide the incoming orders into thousandths of a second and filter the orders accordingly, are you able to assign these cumulative orders to a single market participant. Of course, the big players also know that the cumulative orders are not easy to identify. So when a large buy market order comes into the market, many believe that a big player wants to push the market up. Then many buyers jump into the market with buy market orders, the big player absorbs the market orders with his sell limit orders and then pushes the market down. So if you see a large, non-cumulative order in the market, you should always be careful. With the right trading software, it is first of all quite easy to differentiate these cumulative and non-cumulative market orders. But be careful, a big player does not always have to be responsible when a large cumulative market orders appears in the market.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Here we see a situation on the Euro FX 30 Sec Chart. At point A, the price is pushed down and the first stops (cumulative market orders) of the long traders are triggered. At Point B, many are hoping for an upward trend, but the price will be pushed down again. Now strong cumulative market orders come in, which are intercepted by buy limit orders from the big player. The big player then pushes the price up with buy market orders. These cumulative market orders were not invested by the big player, but show that the stops of the long traders were close to each other. The big players need this liquidity because the retail trailers are rarely willing to deliver so much volume at the same price level. For this reason, stophunting is a crucial factor for the big players. The orders we see in this picture are only market orders.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The information about limit orders is very sparse or not available in most trading platforms. Basically, you can display ten price levels in the sell limit and buy limit range in most trading platforms. For a lot of money, it is possible on some exchanges to display more price levels in the limit area. Anyone who has ever dealt with limit orders in the DOM knows that this view is of little use. Depending on the volatility, the price changes are so fast that added or subtracted limit orders cannot be recognized. With the right algorithms you are able to represent spoofing more precisely. In this example we see an average of 50 lots at each price level, but it happens that 200 lots are sometimes traded at a price level. This means that 150 lots have been added to the limit area. And this can only be seen in the running DOM with a spoofing algorithm. Even if you can see absorption, it doesn't help at first. The big players collect in the accumulation and distribution phases and absorption does not necessarily mean that the price has to move more in the opposite direction afterwards. This will happen after the big players have collected enough. Another option to make the limit order visible is the heat map, whereby the subdivision of the individual limit orders is shown in color. Again, there are some restrictions to be aware of.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

A completely new market view

It should be noted that this presentation is a medium-term to long-term orientation and that no short-term price changes can be derived from it. But if you have this information, you can derive a history from the price trend and use it to forecast a further price trend more precisely. However, only if you are able to see exactly what the big players are aiming for with this procedure. A completely new market view

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Let us first take a closer look at volume and liquidity. The market orders move the market by meeting the limit orders. Here it is crucial how strong the market orders are on the one hand and how strong the limit orders are. First, I assigned three different values to the market orders and limit orders. The value 3 shows a strong tendency, the value 2 a medium tendency and the value 1 a weak tendency.

Now let's look at the first three examples above.

Buy 1

If the buy market orders show a strong tendency and at the same time the sell limit orders also, a preliminary equilibrium results. The volatility would be weak as there would be no major price changes in this case.

Buy 2

If the buy market orders have a strong tendency and the sell limit orders have a medium strength, this results in a preliminary bullish trend. The volatility would be medium, since in this case there will be medium price changes.

Buy 3

If the buy market orders have a strong trend and the sell limit orders have a weak strength, this results in a provisionally strong bullish trend. The volatility would be high, because in this case there will be strong price changes.

The volatility is always the result of the strength or weakness of the limit and market orders. The market orders can move the market, but they cannot stop it. The limit orders cannot move the market, but they can stop it. Both factors therefore determine volatility and future price changes.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Since breakouts are primarily associated with high volatility, we recognize that these breakouts rarely occur in this market. In over 70% of cases, a market is in equilibrium or in a sideways phase. In order to find out exactly how a trend or volatility could develop in the future, it is crucial to identify the strength of the market orders and at the same time the strength of the limit orders. The strength of the market orders is relatively easy to see. Why volume trading doesn't work

Hello dear subscribers,

In my last post I tried to identify volume and liquidity. We have found that liquidity determines the market.

Volume versus liquidity

An idea first emerged from this:

As it looks, we will have to identify the limit orders with our own algorithms, which could result in indicators that tell us the respective strength in the limit area. This strength in the limit area must then be compared with the strength in the market area in order to project a result. This would enable us to specifically determine the result of supply and demand. I would like to take a closer look at this today and formulate my idea a little more precisely.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

As we know, the Sell Market Order (Point A) is an active order that moves the market and meets the passive Buy Limit Order (Point B). The limit order is only able to stop the market. For this reason, this area is referred to as the offer market. The buy market order (point C) is an active order that moves the market and meets the passive sell limit order (point D). The sell limit order is only able to stop the market. For this reason, this area of the market is called the demand market. Since only the market orders can move the market, the description of supply and demand is initially correct, but if we note that the limit orders are able to stop the market orders, this results in another possibility of determining supply and demand.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Let us first take a closer look at the different zones of supply and demand.

Point A

In the offer area there is a 20 Lot Market Sell Order that meets the Limit buy order. For a better overview I have marked the 20 lots with a minus sign.

Point B

The 20 Lot Market Sell Order now meets a 70 Lot Limit buy order. The limit buy order is so large that it completely absorbs the market sell order and if no further market sell orders come into the market, no price change will take place downwards. That's why Limit Sell is a demand market for me.

Point C

In order for another price change to take place, another 50 Lot Market Sell Orders would have to run into the Limit buy order. Since the limit buy order has the ability to stop the market sell order, I have called the limit buy order a demand. In this case, the bearish result is rather bullish as the market sell order failed to penetrate the limit buy order.

Point D

A market buy orders of 60 lots runs into a sell limit orders of 50 lots.

Point E

First, the market buy orders eats 50 lots in the limit sell orders and after it is used up, the price changes by a tick upwards. If the limit sell orders above this is greater than ten lots and no further market buy orders enter the market, the market buy order is also initially held there. That's why Limit Sell is an offer market for me.

Point F

The bullish result would initially be 10 lots bigger, since the market buy order has completely eaten up the limit sell order and has slid into the next price level.

Point G

We initially have two offer markets, one that is the market sell order, which is able to eat up the limit buy order and at the same time the limit sell order, which is able to hold up the market buy order. Together, these two types of orders would have a strength of 70 lots. If we add the two demand markets together, we come to a strength in the demand area of 130 lots.

Point H

The result of supply and demand would be 60 lots and therefore bullish overall. The demand market is therefore stronger overall.

My idea is based on the fact that although a market orders can move the market, it is not able to stop it. A limit orders cannot move the market, but it can stop it. Each different Market- or Limit orders has a strength and a weakness. For this reason, the idea arose to give each different order the name supply or demand. A total strength of supply and demand can be determined from the offsetting.

This approach is actually quite logical, because if strong market buy orders come in to push the market up, the limit buy orders would also have to form more strongly to hedge the price down. Because if there was a breakout upwards and the limit buy side would not slide up with a stronger liquidity, some lots in the market sell area would ensure that the price would go completely down again. The limit buy area is therefore a clear indicator of a demand market. That would mean that supply and demand cannot be determined solely with market orders. Given that the big players work almost exclusively with limit orders, this conclusion is clearly logical.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Point A

As I have already written, the information passed on in the area of active market orders is absolutely precise and sufficient to precisely calculate strength, volatility and many other factors.

Point B

In the area of market orders, it is very easy to identify cumulative orders from the big players. This is done with algorithms that are able to summarize orders that were placed within 1/1000 second and display them as a large order. The big players like to use these cumulative market orders to push the market upwards and not to be recognized at the same time. These cumulative orders are not easy to identify, but with the right tools it is possible.

Point C

Orders that are not accumulated are often used by big players to mislead the market, or at the same time, provide yourself with liquidity. When a large market order comes in that is not absorbed at the same time, it is often a market deception. Many market participants see this large order and at the same time invest in the same market direction. This enables the big player to sell his large order to retail traders in small quantities and then push the market down.

Point D

There are sufficient tools and algorithms to identify cumulative and non-cumulative market orders and to assign them to individual market participants.

Point E

In the area of passive orders (limit sell or limit buy orders), identification is significantly more difficult. Of course, we know that a buy market order automatically activates a sell limit order, but at first it is not clear who accepted the sell limit order.

Point F

Cumulative ticks in the area of passive limit orders are also called iceberg orders. Big players often rightly fear that simply displaying their limit orders could move the price and that other market participants could use the large order volume to their advantage. This is why big players are able to bring a large order to the limit page, although only a small part of this order is always shown in the order book. The total volume remains invisible. If a peak is executed, the next peak appears in the system and so on. The algorithms are responsible for the fact that new peaks are constantly being added and that the apparently small limit order is able to strongly absorb market oders.

Point G

As soon as there is more liquidity in the DOM on the limit side, this should be viewed with great caution. The big player knows that this large limit order can be seen by every market participant. If a large limit sell order suddenly appears in the market, many assume that the market cannot continue to move upwards because the market cannot break through this strong order. Shortly before execution, the big order is deleted by the big players and the price continues to rise sharply. This is also a way to eliminate long traders.

Point H

Iceberg orders are generally not identifiable, but the big players  reveal themselves as soon as they activate the algorithms that prepare an iceberg order. These algorithms can be identified in the headmap and indicate a possible iceberg order. With my spoofing tool I am able to recognize added or subtracted limit orders within the DOM. However, most market participants will not be able to see the limit orders. And that is exactly why the big players work almost exclusively with these limit orders.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

In order to determine whether the big player is making its own liquidity available, you have to work with a headmap. The strong green bars at Point A are large buy limit orders that simultaneously absorb strong market sell orders (red circles and triangles). To work with this view, you need special algorithms that show you cumulative and non-cumulative market orders. With this view you already have clear advantages over most market participants

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Point A and B

Here we see the possibility to identify spoofing within the DOM. It is possible to keep an eye on the current spoofing and at the same time the accumulated spoofing. Point A shows spoofing in the buy limit area and Point B shows spoofing in the sell limit area.

Point C

Another interesting possibility is to show the current liquidity on the sell limit orders and buy limit orders page with a special time and sales list. This enables you to determine whether liquidity is increasing or decreasing on a certain side.

Point D

Another good option is to look at the cumulative volume with the associated delta. Since every market order runs into a limit order, you are able to enter the delta in the limit area relatively quickly.

Point E

Another very helpful point is to look at the market orders as soon as a big player pushes the price in a certain direction. To do this, you have to commission algorithms to filter out certain cumulative order groups, which can also be made audible with tones. This can also be used to identify stops by retail traders.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Here we see the last 3 hours in Euro FX, from Friday in the limit delta area. The green lines show the delta in the buy limit area, while the red lines show the delta in the sell limit area. The blue background shows the total volume. At this point the following recommendation can be made: If you are working with a volume profile, leave it in the future. The volume is an interesting piece of information to see in which area there have been strong price wars, but the volume is only the total result of bid and ask. Many now think that if the volume on the ask side has gained, the price will continue to go up. However, this is a big mistake, because the limit orders are decisive, because the big players use them to collect bid or ask and exit the market with limit orders. At point A and B we see a strong sell limit delta that was formed. As of 9:15 p.m. CET, the price dropped 40 pip.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The same currency pair, in the same time unit, with a slightly more precise representation. The green bars show the buy limit orders, the red bars the sell limit orders in the delta. The numbers on the left show the number in seconds how long the price stayed within the respective price level. The total volume can also be easily derived from this.

Volume trading has grown significantly in importance in recent years and there are many statements on how to trade volume. But in my opinion, this path is completely wrong. The big players collect and sell only in the limit area, they only use the volume to push the price in a certain direction. Retail traders primarily work with volume and less with liquidity. Therefore, only liquidity decides on the medium-term and long-term course. Of course, short-term price movements can also be derived from the volume, but if you want to make profits in the long term, you should therefore be guided by liquidity. And that is exactly why I am a liquidity trader and not a volume trader.

If you want to follow the big players, you should therefore concentrate more on liquidity than volume. However, since we receive very little information in the liquidity area, we can determine the liquidity by volume. But you should never act according to volume, because then you are on the wrong side.

This automatically leads to a truth that should make retail traders think. The retail traders primarily deal with the volume that can be identified by everyone in the market. The big players primarily deal with liquidity that no one in the market can identify. So the big players see what we do, but we don't see how the big players act. I leave it to your imagination whether this is just a coincidence.

I hope that I was able to clarify a few things, wish you a great weekend and a great trading success in the next week.

Lovely wishes

Michael

The Truth of successful Liquidity Traders

Hello dear subscribers,

In my post yesterday I showed why a volume trader is in most cases wrong and volume trading cannot work in the long run.

Why volume trading doesn't work

Of course, it is generally better to get a volume from the exchange market than a tick volume from the forex market. I have specifically described the differences here.

Volume in forex

First of all, the volume from the stock market is nothing more, as the total of Bid and Ask. With the volume, we can see how many market buy orders and market sell orders came into the market at one price level, but only total. Even if we differentiate the volume by color, it only tells us which market orders were outnumbered. The only important information from a high volume is the fact that a price war has taken place there. No more and no less. Deriving a possible winner from this is pure speculation and does not help us. As we already know, the market orders move the price in the short term, but the limit orders actually determine the long-term price trend. I have created two examples for you.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Here we see a price trend in the Euro FX M15 with a delta liquidity. The green bars show the buy limit orders, the red bars the sell limit orders. First the course ran from top to bottom and an equilibrium formed. Within this equilibrium there were two zones in which strong buy limit orders were activated. Prize question: What do you think, where the course will go in the medium term?

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

You probably already guessed it, the course went up clearly. Of course, the price broke out of the zone a few times within the equilibrium, but take a look at zones A to E to see what type of limit orders were activated and how the price reacted to them. This is crucial information that will give you a significant market advantage.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

We remain in the Euro FX M15 and see that the price initially rose and an equilibrium forms again. Within this equilibrium there were again two zones, in which mainly sell limit orders were activated. Question: What do you think where the course could go in the medium term?

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The representation in this volume profile is absolutely correct, because in these areas more market buy orders than market sell orders have actually entered the market. Since we know that the big players collect almost exclusively in the limit orders area, we can assume that these market buy orders were absorbed by the limit sell orders. The volume trader sees in this overview that the market buy orders were clearly outnumbered. Of course, you could now say that the market buy orders in Zone B tried to push the price up a lot, but failed. For this reason, one could assume that the market buy orders were absorbed. The decisive factor, however, is the fact that looking at market buy orders leads you in the wrong direction.

How a big player turns his position

Hello dear subscribers,

Already in mid-February I noticed that the big players are increasingly making their own liquidity available. I was initially unable to classify this because a hedge, apart from double costs, does not offer any advantage at first. But if you are more concerned with the way big players work, you quickly understand that this approach has interesting aspects for big players.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

On February 19, 2020, I reported for the first time on a situation where the big players made themselves available liquidity. A few days later, at the same price level, a few hours apart, there were two situations in which two big players each provided over 1,000 lots of their own liquidity.

On the trail of the big players

Own liquidity for the big players

In the past, the big players had to collect ask or bid within an equilibrium, very elaborately in different price levels. The big effort is to keep the course within this range. If Ask is collected in an accumulation phase and the price then rises sharply, it must be pushed down again by the big players. To do this, the dollar must first be bought. As soon as the price has reached the lower range, the dollar has to be sold. ASK is required for this. However, this ASK cannot be collected because it is needed to exit the dollar. The big player only has the chance to collect the necessary ASK within a downward movement with buy limit orders. In an upward movement it is much harder to get ASK, unless the big player manages to trigger the short trader's stops. Collecting within an equilibrium is a very time-consuming and expensive effort to get the necessary Bid or Ask. A report on Goldman Sachs, who have reduced their daily income by 30% in the past five years, shows that this approach has become increasingly difficult in recent years.

Problems for the big players?

The big players have the power to move the markets in their given direction, the only disadvantage they have had so far is the fact that they were not able to immediately buy 2000 Lot Ask or Bid and then move the price in their direction. In the following article you can read again the advantages and disadvantages of retail traders / big players.

Follow Smart Money !!!

With the experiment: own liquidity, you have tried to eliminate this disadvantage in recent weeks. The way it looks, it seems to be paying off for the big players, as their own liquidity has been provided very often in recent weeks. In terms of cost, this should not be a major disadvantage, because if you collect within an equilibrium, the course must be kept within a range over a certain period of time. On the one hand this is very time consuming and on the other hand it is very risky because e.g. 2000 Lot Ask will be invested, for several days in the market . If, due to a special market situation, a price slump occurs, it is questionable whether the big player will be able to push the price up again. This could result in significant losses.

If a big player brings a market buy order of 2000 lots into the market, which he picks up at the same time as a 2000 lot sell limit order, he initially only has twice the cost. There is no loss in a price movement because it is a hedge. First he can analyze the market and find out in which direction the dump money is heading. The big player can then take the opposite position and push the course strongly in one direction through the triggered stops. At some point he has to make a decision and get out of a position. At this moment, the big player still has no profit since the second position is now in the minus. Now the course has to be pushed back in the opposite direction and got out of position at the given time.

If a big player has collected for a long time, this resulted in a larger equilibrium and then there was a stronger price movement up or down. If he provides himself with liquidity, e.g. this resulted in a strong upward trend and after in a strong downward trend. This creates a significantly higher volatility than in the first case. Of course, once a big player has provided himself with liquidity, he can get out of a position as quickly as possible and then push the price in the opposite direction. In my opinion, these different experiments are currently running in EURUSD. The big players are trying to find out which strategy is cheaper and more efficient. If this strategy were to succeed, the equilibrium in the EURUSD would be drastically reduced. The big players would be able to buy a large number of ask or bid more quickly and could push the price up or down faster.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

I analyzed the range of the last 28 trading days in EURUSD. Point A shows the time when I noticed that the big players started their experiment. For this reason, I have examined the 14 trading days before and the 14 trading days after.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The red fields show the range of 14 trading days before the start of the experiment and the green fields show the range of 14 trading days after the start of the experiment. It is striking that the range has more than doubled. It can also be seen that less equilibrium developed in the second period.

Now you have to consider fairly, of course, that we have had a special market situation in the past 14 days, not least because of the scaremongering of the corona virus. Due to the resulting economic restrictions in many areas, the markets are currently very volatile and unpredictable. Therefore, the price of the course in EURUSD cannot be assigned exclusively to this experiment.

First of all, it remains to be seen whether this approach will be confirmed by the big players in the future, and then we will do another calculation. However, the fact is that an equilibrium significantly reduces volatility. If the number of equilibrium in EURUSD is reduced, this could result in significantly higher volatility. But it is too early for this speculation, we should wait and see how the market develops in the future. So far, the EURUSD was one of the safest currency pairs, the volatility was in the middle and had very little drawdowns. Should the number of equilibrium decrease significantly, future drawdowns could increase significantly.

There is another point that has been a major disadvantage for big players in the past. When the big player had collected a certain number of bids within the equilibrium, there was initially a small breakout to eliminate possible short traders. Then the course was pushed down. The long trader's stops were triggered and used to accelerate the price down faster. You also have to pay attention if a price movement has gone down sharply in a downward trend. Then the big player pushes the price up sharply to trigger the stops of the short traders. He also intercepts these with his sell limit orders in order to obtain further liquidity. As soon as he pushes the price down again, the stops of the long traders are triggered, which push the price further down. This is how the big player manages to push the course down over a long distance.

The problem with the big players in the past was that they had to step out of their 2,000 lot position at some point to realize their winnings. To sell the dollar they need Ask. They can only get ASK, if other market participants are willing to buy BID, because they believe that the market will continue to slide. In the past, this means that the big players usually had to exit their positions well before the low. If they go out of their position on the low, they might not found any market participants to buy the dollar from them.

This is actually very ineffective when a price goes down 100 pip, but a big player has to get out at 65 pip. The big players have come up with another experiment for this. I would like to describe this procedure as: turn position. This situation arose yesterday and I would like to briefly describe it.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

First of all, we see the course of yesterday's price. From the daily open it went down to -105 pip, then 70 pip up, 70 pip down, 60 pip up, and then 100 pip down. This time, a big player tried to took this 100 pip completely.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Around 5:45 p.m., there were already massive exits by some big players out of the dollar. We can see that large limit buy orders have already entered the market, that have absorbed the sell market orders. This initially ensured that the market went up again. The big player that was still in the market with its big Lot position, pushed the market down again. At Point B, no participant was willing to place additional sell market orders on the market. The big player placed several cumulative buy market orders totaling 2000 lots, which he simultaneously absorbed with his own 2000 lot sell limit order. This move was absolutely smart because it sold its 2,000 lot position to itself. At that point, I was in front of a screen with a friend and told him that the price would now like to go up a lot, but it won't go up because the big player has to get out of his euro. It was the same way.

Because the big player at point B brought a total of 2000 lots of cumulative buy market orders to the market, a lot of traders with a long position jumped on this move. It looked like a lot of different traders took a long position. This created a herd instinct. Everyone wants to be there. The green circles at Point C are all market orders that have entered this equilibrium. Interestingly, they didn't move the price up much. That was also clear, because the big player with his sell limit orders ensured that he came out of his upside-down euro position. That initially held up the price.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

In this situation, we took a closer look at the bid and ask. We noticed that the delta was positive in the beginning. This means that the big player initially absorbed fewer market buy orders and allowed the price to rise slightly. Had he brutally tried to get out of his position, he would have stop the market up. That would have prevented further buyers from entering the market and the price could have gone down again.

Thus, the big player managed to get out of his euro position little by little and overall he was able to realize a greater profit, than if he had exit the dollar at the range of 70%.

Of course, this situation could have happened completely differently, this representation is only my own interpretation. However, my own interpretation speaks for a significantly higher profit on the part of the big players. And since the big players are only profit-oriented in the market, there is a high probability that my interpretation could contain a great deal of truth. When this situation arose, it was clear to me that I would not be entering into a long trade at this point because I could assume that the big player wanted to get out of its euro position. Why should I use a long position to help the big player get out of his position?

If this approach accumulated in the future, an equilibrium at the end of the day could be identified as a possible exit for the big players. This strategy would accelerate the EURUSD and we would no longer have to wait for the breakout in the Equilibrium for days. That means more potential profits in less time. This will also increase the number of breakouts. But it doesn't make the market any easier, quite the opposite.

The truth about the volume profile

Hello dear subscribers,

As we know, there has been a huge increase in volume trading in recent years. Many trainers have specialized in this and give their students absolutely wrong information about the volume profile. In my last articles I already pointed out that the volume profile does not provide any specific information in order to obtain concrete trading advantages. Today I want to show you what information you get from a volume profile and why you should rather do without it.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Here we see a volume profile in the Euro FX H1 over a period of 20 hours. First of all, a volume profile is nothing more than the addition of ask and bid at the respective price level. There are price levels where there is an increased volume and price levels where there is only a small volume. This allows you to determine the price level at which an increased price war has taken place. It is not clear who won the price war and why. There are many different interpretations within this volume profile, which in my opinion represent pure speculation. Anyone working in this market should not rely on speculation, but rather rely solely on facts. Of course, the backward interpretation of a volume profile is simple, but the goal should be to derive a future price trend from a current volume profile. And that is only possible with interpretation. So the volume profile is no concrete help.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Here we see a colored volume profile, the red bars show that the bid and the green bars show that the ask were outnumbered. However, you can also do relatively little with this information. If 1000 Lot Ask and 1001 Lot Bid were traded at one price level, a large red bar with 2001 Lot volume is displayed. This view gives us completely wrong information at the moment, in fact the number of market buy orders and market sell orders was almost identical.

At Point A, a volume of over 3300 lots was achieved, the ask side had the upper hand. Now, of course, one could say that these ask were absorbed and the price has therefore gone down. It's always easy to explain in the past perspective, but why didn't the course at Point B go down? In addition, it is strange that such a large absorption took place at precisely one price level. The probability tends towards zero that two different big players take an opposite position at the same price level.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

We now go one step further and look at the delta volume. This delta volume is calculated by the market orders by displaying ask minus bid. So it shows the result of the respective winner. At points A and B there was a surplus of 2800 and 2400 lots on the ask side. At Point C we also find a surplus on the ask page of over 2000 lots. First of all, this information does not help us, because every market order runs into a limit order.

Either the market buy order manages to eat its way through the limit sell order and further increase the price, or the brand buy order is absorbed by the limit sell order. This representation here shows only the delta of the market orders. The market orders move the market, but are unable to hold a price. As I have already written in many articles, the big players primarily work with limit orders because within one equilibrium they collect a certain number of Bid or Ask .

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

For this reason, I only show the liquidity in my delta chart. This liquidity is calculated by the limit orders, whereby ask minus bid is also calculated here. Liquidity is the optimal indicator of a long-term price movement. In my view, the yellow arrow absorbed 2800 lots in the sell limit area. It is crucial to find out first of all how this absorption could take place at all.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

It is necessary to work with the DOM and the time and sales list. There I get all the information about the different market orders received. A distinction can be made between cumulative market orders (point A) and non-cumulative market orders (point B). It is crucial to identify a possible algorithm.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

In the footprint chart we see that in the buy market area 2681 lots were absorbed at one price level. In contrast, the number of market sell orders was very small in the same period. The number of market sell orders at this moment indicates the more realistic market. This means that something special must have happened at this price level.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

For this we first need an individually configured heat map that shows us the limit orders and the market orders at the same time. I already reported in mid-February that the big players, in a kind of experiment, are providing themselves with liquidity in order to eliminate the disadvantage of tedious collecting in the equilibrium. If 2000 lot market buy orders are simultaneously absorbed by 2000 lot limit sell orders at a the same price level, it cannot be a coincidence. No big player can know that another big player brings a certain number of market orders into the market at precisely one price level. Even if he could guess that, this absorption would take place over several price levels. In this way, the specific coincidence can be excluded and it is quite obvious that this is a matter of obtaining liquidity in-house.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Let's first look at what exactly happened. At Point A, the big player made himself available volume in the form of 2000 lot market buy orders, which he also absorbed with 2000 lot limit sell orders. Many participants saw that strong buy market orders entered the market and entered into a long trade. When the price was pushed down, the stops of these long traders helped accelerate the price down. Then the price was pushed to point B. There the big player got out of his 2000 lot dollar position. At Point C he bought another 500 Lot Limit buy orders and pushed the price to Point D. The same game was played there again. The traders now believed that the price could go up and were stopped because the price was running back. The course ran to Point E and there the big player sold his 4500 Lot Euro position. Now there was only a 2000 lot dollar position open, which was in the red. The price was pushed down to point F where the big player closed his dollar position. Since this strategy took place in the Forex market, the profit was approximately $ 200 million, which probably shared two big players.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

I believe that it becomes clear relatively quickly that a volume chart cannot convey this information. Therefore I recommend not using a pure volume chart. The limit orders determine the medium and long-term market development, so the concentration should be limited to it. In the next few weeks, we will deal more with limit orders and in particular with the Big Players own liquidity. In the past few days we have seen that Asians are strong invest in the euro, this situation is being exploited by the big players, who are making themselves available liquidity in order, to fish the asians profits. The increased volatility that we currently see in EURUSD is therefore based on two factors. On the one hand the fear of the Corona Virus and on the other hand the self-provided liquidity. Only when the panic about the Corona Virus has reduced significantly will we be able to record the specifically increased volatility through the liquidity they have made available. In the future this means less equilibrium and significantly more movements within an increased volatility. Many traders have noticed in the past few days that the markets have changed significantly. It will be a while before the markets normalize again, but if the experiment "own liquidity" go on, it will be much more difficult for most Forex traders to make constant profits. I therefore recommend that you deal with the new situation right now.

Precise information about this begins with this post:

On the trail of the big players

Limit Delta gifts

Hello dear subscribers,

As I have already written, there are two ways of looking at the deltas. We can represent the volume delta and the liquidity delta. For the volume delta, ask minus bid is calculated in the area of the market orders and for the liquidity delta, ask minus bid is shown in the area of the limit orders. A volume analysis is usually carried out with market orders, whereby the ask and bid are added together. It shows us where a price war has taken place, but the consequences of this cannot be deduced.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

First the price went up to point A. The volume was relatively low and suddenly I saw a sell limit delta of 279 lots forming at one price level, the price went down again and took a second attempt at point B. The total volume was again very small and increased slightly when the course came to Point B. A sell limit delta of 84 lots was now formed at the same price level. Although this was significantly lower than the previous Sell Limit Delta, it was already above average in relation to the deltas within the candle. Here a clear absorption could be identified, which then pushed the price down by 30 pip.

The price ran into Zone C, where strong buy limit orders entered the market two hours earlier. For this reason, I have drawn this zone as a possible purchase zone. What was decisive for me, however, was how the buy limit delta would behave within this zone. At first an equilibrium was formed and it was found that further buy limits were collected within this zone. Then the course from point D to point E was pushed up. Interestingly, there was a stronger absorption at point E, which pushed the price down another 20 pip. But the stronger buy limit orders from zone C had to be brought into profit, so the price was pushed further up.

Then the course ran to Point F and we see that at Point F & G there was again a stronger absorption which pushed the course down another 25 pip. I marked zones A, B and E as the exit. The price actually went up again afterwards.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

A special variant is the consideration of the limit delta within a certain zone. When the price went up to point A, a strong sell limit delta zone was formed at point B and a strong buy limit delta zone at point C. We can then determine that the subsequent equilibrium moved exactly within this zone. Only with a strong penetration at Point D did the course accelerate downwards.

Looking at the delta in the sell limit and buy limit area is very interesting information that helps us traders in many areas. However, we have to be careful with this information, as the limit area is always long-term. This means that the price does not react immediately to the sell limit orders, but often with a slight delay. It can also happen that a stop running takes place in order to eliminate possible short or long traders. This presentation is a very good overview to understand what is currently happening in the market.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The medium-term consideration can be optimally recorded with a limit delta chart in M5 (point A) and a heat map (point B). This allows you to identify the stophunting as well as exceptional situations when a big player makes his own liquidity available. Point C shows the exact situation again, how the market orders run into the limit order.

I make my actual trading decisions based on short-term information. With point D and E I find the individual algorithms of the market orders on the buy and sell side. I have these algorithms displayed by two different tones that come in in milliseconds. The data is also shown to me, but since I concentrate on limit orders, the tones help me as a third dimension. So I can very quickly determine whether a buy algorithm is absorbed by the sell limit or eats up the sell limit orders.

As additional information, a footprint in the range chart (point F) helps me, where I have hidden the imbalance in the market orders area. This enables me to quickly identify the relevant market orders. Point G shows me the cumulative delta of the day in connection with the open interest, i.e. all open long positions.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

In parallel, I keep an eye on the currency strength from the Forex market, the ATR, the Stophunting in the H4 and all relevant meetings of the day that can lead to increased volatility. However, the information from the forex market is significantly slower than the identified algorithms in the future market.

At first glance, my 8 trading screens seem very confusing for a beginner. My big advantage is that I only represent one currency pair there and save a lot of time because I don't have to constantly switch to other time units. 67% of the screen area gives me information from the future market, while the remaining 33% are reserved for the forex market. However, it also took me many years to find the optimal display and changes take place every day because the market is constantly changing. I can always use two screens for these experiments and still do my trading. Our fiber optic cable is already in the house, I hope that the connection will be made soon in order to achieve a significantly better ping time. Another advantage will be the download / upload of 1000/500 Mbit, since the amount of data can be better distributed to my different workstations via a LAN cable. A professional workplace costs some money, but saves a lot of time in the long term. Because time is money. With a Porsche, you can also achieve better lap times at the Nürburgring than with a conventional vehicle. But you have to be ready to invest.

From this long-term and medium-term information, I first have to present a story that I compare with the Stophunting from the Forex market. From this, I first identify buy and sell zones, which I draw on the chart. Once the course comes into my created zones, the response of the algorithms is the deciding factor. After that, I decide relatively quickly whether I want to enter the market or not. My exit is also shaped by the short-term information, whereby I also consider the medium-term information to let profits run. I work with very small stops of 2.5 pip, which requires a 100% entry shortly before a small breakout up or down. In extremely volatile phases, I let the price come back again because this is to stop the traders who are right. As soon as this area has been cleaned up by the big players, you can easily be dragged up or down. Therefore, it is rarely advisable to get in after a strong movement. Of course, I am also stopped if I have worked too imprecisely. But thanks to my future data, this rate has halved. While I used to trade in equilibrium, today I tend to take the more volatile side. This generates more pip per minute and drastically reduces the time spent in the market. However, due to my financial situation, I am not forced to make daily profits. This takes a lot of pressure out and promotes the fun of trading. I prefer a loss that I can understand than a gain that is inexplicable to me. In any case, you should only trade with money that you could easily do without.

Trading successfully in Forex is one of the biggest challenges. The opponents that stand in our way are the best traders in the world. It is perfectly clear that you will pay your tuition fees in the first few years with losts. If you keep your losses small, are willing to learn, question your setup every day and stick it out, you have the best chance of living on it in the long term. In this blog you will find many ideas that can save you a lot of time so as not to repeat the mistakes we long-time traders have all made.
