--- 帖子 #1425 ---
The law of the market economy

Hello dear subscribers,

There are many providers in the forex and stock market that offer software, data feeds, indicators, EA's, training courses or trading signals. Many offers are unnecessary, too expensive, or fraudulent. How do I find the best product for me now? In order to explain the optimal procedure, let's first look at an example of how to find a good winter tire.

When driving, the tire contact area, i.e. the area that touches the road, is only about the size of a palm. These few centimeters have to carry a car weighing several tons and protect the most important content, humans, from unpleasant accidents. For this it is important to use a high quality tire. How do I find the best winter tire now? All-weather tires are out of the question because they are comparable to a duck. The duck can run, fly and swim, with certain restrictions. But she can't swim, run, or fly well.

Interestingly, there are many test reports from different winter tires, some of which are sponsored by tire manufacturers. Everything is analyzed, liability in snow, liability in ice, liability in water, liability in dry conditions, abrasion, rolling noise, guarantee, price and much more. Then points are awarded and there is a winner and a loser. Depending on the weighting of the points, every winter tire can theoretically be named the winner.

I am only interested in the grip and braking distance in wet, snow and ice. From this I create the best winter tire for me. As soon as I have filtered out the best winter tire, it is about the price comparisons. I always buy my winter tires in midsummer and my summer tires in winter. Since our market always responds to the subject of supply and demand, I can save up to 50%.

The time required for this saving is limited, the only disadvantage is that you have to buy the tires half a year before using them. But when it comes to saving, this disadvantage also works in my favor. Of course, this procedure also works with the topic: data feed, stock exchange software, brokers and many other things in everyday life.

If you are interested in a data feed, you should first research the Internet. If we assume that there are 10 different data feeds, then one can assume that 20% are expensive, 60% on average and 20% are inexpensive. First of all, it is important to determine an average price for a product. But the decisive factor is not the price, but the performance. What is the use of a cheap data feed that fails permanently or provides me with inaccurate values? That is why the optimal price-performance ratio is the decisive factor.

The Internet provides this information, although you should neglect the first results on Google, since it is usually only paid advertising. First, look for comparisons or warnings about certain products. Of course, good products sometimes have bad ratings, but good products always prevail. The book Harry Potter has a 5-star rating, although some of the 10,000 ratings have also given negative votes. When you buy something, you should first know exactly what you need. You should have the necessary expertise to do this. If you do not have the necessary specialist knowledge, you can look at the recessions of experts and thus form an opinion more quickly. This takes some time, but prevents money loss by making a decision too quickly.

There is an interesting law of business that the English writer and social philosopher John Ruskin created many years ago.

There is hardly anything in the world that not anyone can make a little worse and sell a little cheaper, and people who only focus on price become the just prey of such people. It is unwise to pay too much, but it is even worse to pay too little. If you pay too much, you lose some money, that's all. On the other hand, if you pay too little, you sometimes lose everything because the item purchased cannot perform its intended purpose. The law of the economy forbids to get a lot of value for little money. If you accept the lowest offer, you have to add something for the risk you take. And if you do that, you have enough money to pay for something better.

For this reason, you should always try to find the best price-performance ratio. For some it is the most expensive, for the second the best quality, for the third the cheapest for the fourth the easiest handling and so on. It is crucial that you are satisfied with your decision for the next few years and can look forward to it every day.

I wish you always make the right decisions.

best regards

Michael

[quote=Sesamstrasse;12882834]Moin Michael. I really like to see your examples on live trades.

Hello Guido,

First of all, I would like to congratulate you on taking on this not easy challenge. It takes some time to have stock market data translated by a prop software. The problem here is the infinite number of possibilities that arise with the filter settings. First of all, I would concentrate on limit orders as they determine the future course of the market. Sell market orders runs in buy limit orders and  buy market orders runs in sell limit orders. The stock market data initially only show us the market orders. But we know that a market order can only be activated if it is simultaneously accepted by a limit order. This can be used to represent a limit order by simply swapping the color. So if a buy market order (green) runs into a sell limit order (red), I can display the limit orders by changing the color. This creates a small challenge. If 100 lot buy market orders are accepted by sell limit orders, you have to assume that not all sell limit orders belong to a single big player. The big players usually use triggered stops to fill their limit orders. Therefore, the market orders must first be sorted according to triggered stops in order to present them as decisive limit orders. Then the limit orders must be assigned to individual big players. First of all, this is a bigger challenge that we have already dealt with. The main thing here is to determine a future market direction with the decisive limit orders. The short-term movements can then be determined relatively easily using the 4D strength method described.

Act in the eye of the tornado

There is an exception if a big player makes volume available to himself that he absorbs with his own limit orders at the same time. This procedure does not initially show a clear direction of the big player, which can, however, be determined with a certain delay. This can then be used to derive specific price levels that show us exactly where the future course is headed. This "own liquidity strategy" has only been used increasingly since the beginning of the Corona crisis and it will still take some time before the big players have developed a concrete strategy from it. However, this procedure is very easy to identify and just as easy to act on. For this reason, I hope that this strategy will become an integral part of the big player strategy in the future.

In this market, we will never be able to specifically determine which goal is being pursued with market orders and limit orders. But even if our assumptions are only 50% correct, this will significantly improve the probability of winning and at the same time reduce losses. Another advantage is the market advantage. If, in the second half of an equilibrium, ask was increasingly collected with buy limit orders, the price trend is set up. The question is whether long traders with a stophunting have to be switched off beforehand or whether the price goes up immediately. However, this can often be seen from the big players' market orders. A residual risk will always remain, but with very small stops of 1-2 pip a manageable risk.

I wish you a nice weekend and not so much stress for the next 6 weeks of your project.

--- 帖子 #1429 ---
Why candles don't work properly in retail

Hello dear subscribers,

As a beginner, you may know this situation. The price suddenly rises quickly and you would like to take the possible breakout with you. You entry in the middle of the movement, but due to the lack of liquidity, you only get into the market at the end of the big bull candle. As soon as you are in the market the price turns, runs down sharply and you are stopped. You are angry because you were hoping for a breakout and you want to make up for your loss. The price is a new low and it is assumed that the price will now go down more. That's why you spontaneously opt for a short trade. The price actually runs down a bit and you make another short trade to make up for the loss faster. The price stops first and an equilibrium is created. After that, the price slowly goes up, while there are ever stronger down moves in between. These stronger moves down give hope that the trend could continue further down. That is probably why they were ready to pull the stop a bit as the price went higher. Suddenly there was a stronger upward movement and then the price went up 40 pip. The total loss was now as high as if you lost 7 single trades.

The big problem is the candles currently emerging on the market, these often give us the wrong signals, which we also instinctively follow. The biggest delusion is the simple representation of candles by brokers. No matter what time unit we are in, if we look at a past upward trend, we usually see more green candles than red candles, a downward trend shows more red candles than green candles. Green candles show a demand market, red candles show a supply market and dojis show an equilibrium. However, this is a big mistake. The candle gives us traders the wrong truth, which is why the big players rarely work with candles.

Candles are created based on a time-dependent random principle and in the M1 every broker has different candles. An EA based on two moving averages will therefore always achieve different results in the same chart with different brokers. Another factor is the fact that most of the retail traders do not trade in the Forex market at all, but only on a personal platform of the respective broker. Although he receives the Forex price data from a bank, he can pass it on to his customers in various forms. As a rule, trading is carried out on the broker platform, with the broker protecting itself against losses. If 1000 lot short positions and 1500 lot long positions have been placed within a currency, the broker only needs a 500 lot long hedge with the relevant bank to hedge. This means that 2000 lots do not even appear in the real forex market. With ECN brokers it looks different because they forward the relevant trades directly to the Forex market through their bank. This procedure alone can lead to different candle representations.

Many traders get in with a candle movement, green candle long, red candle short and these are typical mistakes that the big players use in their favor. Volume in the form of market orders that meet liquidity in the form of limit orders are the only reason for price movements within a certain time. So the price is the result of volume and liquidity. The time is only a variable factor for the consideration. In the Forex market we only have the time and the price and therefore only the result within a given time (M1, M5 ...). It is crucial to know how the market orders behave compared to the limit orders, and this can only be seen if you receive liquidity volume data. For this reason, I try to largely refrain from displaying candles and to develop modules that show me the strength of market sell orders, market buy orders, limit sell orders and limit buy orders. Time doesn't matter to me, price ist important. I have written a detailed article that I would like to refer to again here.

Bionics 4D strength method

When we see a green candle, we think the market is going up because green means there are more buyers than sellers. But first we should examine this statement in more detail. Market buy orders (ask volume) run into limit sell orders (bid liquidity). When 1 Lot Market Buy Order enters the market, it will be accepted by 1 Lot Limit Sell Order at the same time. If the market is just starting, there are now 2 orders in the market. The market buy order should go up as far as possible, the limit sell order should go down as far as possible. So at this moment there is a buyer and a seller in the market. In a current market, however, it is no longer so easy to determine how many orders, buyers or sellers are actually still in the market.

A green candle is created when the euro is bought or the dollar is sold. And that is a crucial difference. Let us assume that a price has gone down more strongly and a new low has formed. Suddenly a strong green candle emerges. If this candle was created because a market participant bought the euro heavily, the subsequent course of the price is more likely to be bullish than if a market participant sold the dollar at that time. If a market participant gets out of the dollar, he needs Ask. This Ask runs in the sell limit orders and automatically ensures that the price rises. Provided that the orders are large enough to break through the liquidity of the limit orders. If a green candle is formed by a larger market participant getting out of the dollar, it automatically means that he will be out of the market afterwards. With his exit he made sure that a green candle was formed, but it is very likely that he will not invest another Ask to push the price higher.

However, this would be a big exception, since most big players generate their entries and exits almost exclusively via limit orders. Let's stick to the same case. A new low was formed and suddenly a green candle emerged. Then the price jumps upwards and another strong green candle is created.

What could have happened here?

The price was in a downward trend and the big player noticed that too many market participants were short. In order to eliminate these market participants, he has to stop them. To do this, he first buys the euro, pushes the price up and catches the first stops of the short traders. Then a chain reaction occurs. The triggered stops ensure that the price continues to go up and thus trigger further stops that push the price up. The big player waits at this point and absorbs these stops with its limit sell orders previously placed on the market. If necessary, he adds further limit orders via the iceberg orders in order to completely absorb these stops. So he got another cheaper price. As soon as the short traders are out of the market, the big player pushes the price further down.

Let us consider briefly how these two green candles came into being. The first candle was created because the big player bought the euro and pushed the course into the first stops. The second green candle was created because the stops of the short traders were triggered. That means the dollar was selling heavily at that moment. If a price increase is realized due to a dollar sale, there is no basis for an upward price trend. Because to realize a profitable trade upwards, you first need ASK, or buy the euro. Since this was not the case in this case, a long trade could lead to a larger loss. It is precisely for this reason that it is important to know why a green or red candle is created.

Of course I also work with a candle chart (Bionic candle), but only to understand the pricing more quickly. A green candle is initially neutral for me, until I find out whether it is a euro buy or a dollar sale. I only get this information in the stock exchange market. We now know that the big players work almost exclusively with limit orders for their entry and exit and use the market orders to push a price into the first stops, which then trigger a chain reaction. There is an exception if you provide yourself with liquidity, I have already written about this in great detail. Here is the article:

Own liquidity for the big players

Let's stick to the example described, the price is now pushed down by the big player and this triggers the stops of the long traders who started the new up trend with the strong green candle. The big player is now using these stops to get out of his dollar position. Then an equilibrium is created, where the big player first dissolves his remaining dollar position. Another big player is now using this equilibrium to collect a certain number of bid or ask and then push the price in the corresponding direction. And then the same game repeats itself over and over again.

With candle formations it was possible to trade profitably in earlier stock market times, but with the way big players and high-frequency traders work, this is becoming increasingly difficult. Spoofing in the area of limit orders and the use of iceberg orders creates a false representation of supply and demand. The permanent stop hunting for available volume to fill the limit orders changes the structure of the individual candles considerably. A green candle often contains more Bid than Ask and a red candle contains more Ask than Bid. Even with a footprint chart where Bid and Ask stand side by side, the market cannot be analyzed because Bid and Ask have nothing to do with each other. Limit sell orders only cooperate with the market buy orders and limit buy orders only with the market sell orders.

The price is solely the result of this cooperation. And the candle is nothing more than the result of the price. So a candle is just a result, how this result came about is not clear in the Forex market. Anyone who deals with mathematics knows that a result can always be calculated from different factors. And these factors are a crucial point in order to be able to derive possible derivations from them. However, a candle will never be able to help us. However, this proportionality should be considered in order to act profitably.

For the casual trader, the candle is a great way to quickly grasp the market. The brokers benefit from this because a trader would like to have it as simple as possible. The fact that over 90% of traders lose shows that the current representation of the candles is a truth that does not really exist. If you turned the candles exactly, it could lead to a higher success. However, this is pure speculation. Over the years, attempts have been made to improve the appearance of the candles. In principle, Heikin-Ashi is a Japanese representation of price development, similar to candlesticks. Heikin-Ashi was rediscovered in 2003 and means something like balance. It is a type of candle, which shows the prices modified by smoothing them. The advantage of this form of presentation is that trends can be identified more quickly and without tools. After what we know about the candles today, it is only a tool to feel better, I see no concrete advantage due to the lack of information.

The Bionic Candle that I developed should also not be used for entry or exit in the trade, but it has the advantage of conveying faster information. This is crucial to identify the key candle for stophunting. These zones help to determine a possible reversal point in the trend. The decisive factor is the reaction in the area of market and limit orders in order to make a specific trading decision.

Now you could only try to change the scaling of the charts. We would have two options here: In addition to linear chart scaling, charts could also be scaled logarithmically. While the linear chart scaling always refers to absolute numbers, a percentage price movement, in the logarithmic representation, always corresponds to the same distance of the price in the chart. This prevents distortion. However, this also means that we cannot avoid the main problem of the candle.

A friend of mine trades with the same broker as I do, if we work with the same tickchart in the Forex market, different candles are created by the same broker. In the stock market we always have exactly the same information, this are important points that decide between profit and loss. A candle consists of two dimensions: price and time, a market profile in the stock market consists of three dimensions: price, time and volume. The fourth dimension is limit orders and in my eyes the fastest way to capture the market in concrete terms.

Conclusion:

A candle is still the most common representation for analyzing a course or drawing resistance zones. Most Forex indicators are calculated from the price and the time and are basically lagging behind the price. The price is ultimately only the result of the cooperation between market and limit orders. This important information is not available in the Forex market. This automatically brings incorrect information for the individual traders. However, the candle / price in the forex market is the fastest information. Indicators are always lagging and should therefore not be the basis for a trading decision. Since the candle is calculated from the price and the price is only a result, the candle should not be used for a trading decision. Of course there are profitable traders in the Forex market who can successfully trade with candles or indicators. However, this is less due to the specific information that the candles or indicators provide, but more to the many years of experience of these successful traders. There is only one way to trade more profitably: You have to look into the candle but you only get this information with stock market data. Trading on the forex market is a smart way, but only with real stock market data. That is the future for me.

I wish you a great weekend

best regards

Michael

A couple of years back, as an orderflow trader, i set out to compare the "quality" of the data provided by the major data services. My primary focus was on the quality of the data. This would be interesting. For those wanting a deeper dive into this question, straight from the source itself: https://www.cmegroup.com/confluence/...ing+Algorithms . --- 帖子 #1432 ---
Which is stronger, market orders or limit orders?

Hello dear subscribers,

As we have noted, most retail traders do not know why the market they are trading in is moving. However, this is an essential aspect in order to be profitable in the long term. Today's article is about understanding the order flow better and examining two important statements that are conveyed in the market.

1. Market orders move the market, limit orders stop the market.
2. The market moves when more buyers than sellers or sellers are active as buyers.

These statements have burned themselves into the brains of stock market traders over the past 20 years and I would like to show today that these statements are only partially correct. This automatically gives the answer to our question: which is stronger, market orders or limit orders? This answer is a crucial point to concentrate on the essential things in the market.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

A market is determined by supply and demand and the price moves because the market sell orders (point A) run into the limit buy orders (point B) and the market buy orders (point C) into the limit sell orders (point D ) to run. The iceberg orders (point E) lie behind the limit orders and can be replenished if necessary by the big player algorithms in order to absorb further market orders. These facts are known, we have already spoken about them in detail.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Here we see another simplified illustration. The market sell orders (point A) run into the limit buy orders (point B). The first level of limit buy orders in the DOM is the best bid. The market buy orders (point C) run into the limit sell orders (point D). The first level of limit sell orders in the DOM is the best ask. The spread lies between the best ask and the best bid. This spread changes if in a current price, new limit orders are not immediately formed , in the best AsK or Bid. This creates small or larger gaps that are not visible in most cases because they take place inside a candle. First of all, we should think of Point A and B as a car that goes down a mountain, Point C and D being a car that goes up a mountain.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

First we see a red car on the left that wants to drive down. We have to think of the market sell orders at point A as the accelerator pedal of the car. The limit buy orders, we have to think of as the brake of the vehicle. On the right we see a green car that wants to drive up. The market buy orders at point A, we have to imagine as the accelerator pedal of the car. The limit sell orders, we have to think of as the brake of the vehicle.

Let us now assume that the price is on the best bid side. Now 100 Lot Market Sell Orders come into the market, which meet the Limit Buy Orders. If there are now 10 lots on ten levels of the limit buy orders, the 100 lot market sell orders, these ten levels will literally eat up and the price will go down 10 ticks. This means that the market sell orders were at full throttle and the limit buy orders were unable to stop this market sell order.

Now we put the brake on by placing 101 lots on the first level of limit buy orders. The 100 Lot Market Sell Orders now run into the Limit Buy Orders and initially absorb 100 Lot. Now there is still 1 lot on the Limit Buy Order side and since there are no further market sell orders, the price was slowed down. The same example could also be explained with the market buy orders, whereby the vehicle would go up here. So we recognize that we can accelerate the vehicle using the accelerator pedal (market orders) and brake the vehicle using the brake (limit orders). So far, the statement is correct that market orders can move the market and limit orders can stop the market.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Let's ask ourselves two very strange questions. Can you also brake a vehicle with an accelerator pedal and is it possible to accelerate the vehicle with a brake?

From a physical point of view, this is not possible at first, but let us first consider some aspects.

Accelerate with the brake pedal

When a vehicle drives down a slope and you first brake it, it comes to a standstill. If you now release the brake, the vehicle will accelerate due to gravity. Now one would theoretically be able to control the acceleration of the vehicle with a brake.

Braking with the accelerator

When a vehicle drives up a mountain, you have to accelerate first. As soon as I reduce the accelerator pedal force, the vehicle slows down until it may come to a stop. Now you would theoretically be able to control the braking of the vehicle with the accelerator pedal. Even on a straight road, an accelerator pedal would be able to bring a vehicle to a standstill. Let us assume that the vehicle moves slowly forward on an ice surface. You shift into reverse and accelerate slowly. Now the tires on the ice turn in the opposite direction and would theoretically be able to brake the vehicle.

This example should first clarify to us that to a certain extent you can slow down a price with market orders and accelerate a price with limit orders.

How does that work in reality.

Let's say a market is going down and is suddenly stopped by a big player's limit orders. As soon as the big player deletes his limit orders, the market accelerates further downwards. This means that even with limit orders, a big player is able to accelerate or slow down a market.

Let's say that a big player pushes the price up sharply with market orders. Further retail traders follow and help to push the price higher. Suddenly the big player stops his market orders investments, which will slow the price. Now he starts trading a large number of market orders in the opposite direction. As a result, he would be able to completely slow the course upwards. This means that even a big player is able to accelerate or slow down a market with market orders.

The strategies of the big players are controlled using algorithms and ensure that limit and market orders work together at the same time. This results in considerable advantages that the big player can use for himself.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Over the course of a day, we keep seeing that a price suddenly moves up or down quickly without investing a large number of lots. One inevitably wonders how that is possible. The answer lies in programming the big player algorithms.

Let's look at an example. At point A, the big player begins with market buy orders to push the price into the first stops. The subsequent stops are used to push the course further up. The destination is Point C because most stops are suspected there.

The following situation arises at point B. First of all, the big player invests a relatively small number of brand buy orders. When the price was at point A, the big player had already occupied all levels of the sell limit orders between point B and point C. Now the price was at point B. The moment the big player invested his market orders, he also deleted his previously created sell limit orders so that his own market buy orders were able to move upwards. At the same time, the algorithms ensured that strong limit buy orders were placed in the market in order to hedge the price downwards. Now the short traders' first stops were caught and pushed the price further up. The big player now absorbed this ask with his sell limit orders previously placed on the market and was thus able to sell his euro. After that, the market went up a little further, with the big player using this Ask to buy the dollar.

We therefore recognize that the algorithms are optimally coordinated to enable the big player with a small number of lots, large price jumps to catch the first stops. The big player is thus able to achieve the highest possible returns with the least effort.

Now we come to the next statement. The market moves when there are more buyers than sellers or sellers as buyers. This statement is conditionally correct, because let's assume that we have a large number of buyers who place a large number of market buy orders on the market. However, at this price level there is a big player who, with large limit sell orders (iceberg orders), absorbs the complete number of market buy orders. Then we may have a higher number of buyers, but the price doesn't move. Likewise, it would be wrong to say that if there are more buyers than sellers, prices go up and if there are more sellers than buyers, prices go down. The decisive factor here is the interaction between market orders and limit orders that meet.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

In our example we compared the market orders with the accelerator pedal of a vehicle and the limit orders with the brake. Let's first look at what happens in a burnout when we compare the strength of the advance with the brake. In the event of a burnout, the car stops on the spot while the tires turn very quickly. The resulting friction between the tire and the road heats up the rubber, which starts to smoke.

So we recognize first. that the brake is much stronger as the accelerator. If we now transfer this to the market, it becomes clear that the limit orders are far superior to the market orders. This is primarily due to the fact that the big players regulate their entries and exits via limit orders in most cases.

Conclusion:

The price moves because the market sell orders run in the limit buy orders and the market buy orders run in the limit sell orders. The big players collect their ask and bid in the form of limit orders (iceberg orders), as these can hardly be identified in the market. This allows the big players to collect in peace without the majority of traders noticing. The market orders are primarily used to trigger the first stops of retail traders in order to provide themselves with liquidity. Exceptions arise as soon as a big player makes his own liquidity available. Basically, it is correct that market orders move the market, but we should be aware that market orders are also able to stop the market to a certain extent. Basically, it is correct that limit orders can stop the market, but we should be aware that limit orders are also able to move the market.

The fact that the big players primarily work with limit orders leads us to the conclusion that the limit orders are significantly stronger than the market orders. I would even go one step further and make the claim that the limit orders are really moving the market and not the market orders.

If a big player collects a large number of ask during an accumulation phase, it is predictable over a period of time that the price will go up. If a big player collects a large number of bids in a distribution phase, it is foreseeable that the price will then go down. This means that the limit orders specify the medium and long-term price trend. The strong price movements in the market arise primarily from triggered stops by retail traders in order to provide the big players with the appropriate liquidity. Therefore, focusing on market orders is not conducive to long-term profits. In my opinion, the volume trader belongs to an extinct species because it constantly receives incorrect information even in the future market. The future belongs to the liquidity traders who are able to determine the current liquidity of the big players. Because only liquidity shows an experienced trader the future course of the price.

The identification of liquidity is a major challenge because the individual algorithms of the big players must first be decrypted and assigned to the cumulative market orders. The individual strength of the respective market and limit orders based on my 4D strength analysis is very helpful. Additional support can be obtained by identifying the key candle in the Stophunting and the currency strength from the Forex market.

These different tasks will continue to occupy us for the next few months in order to better identify the algorithms of the big players and to derive even more concrete trading advantages from them. The road is hard and rocky and we are making slow progress, but in the end we will say it was worth it.

I wish you a nice Sunday and a successful start to the new trading week

best regards

Michael

Hello simnz,

These are 12 banks and these 12 banks also decide who is primarily served. This is actually logical, because whoever has the house rights will always have an advantage. However, this only applies to limit orders. The following applies in the market orders area: First come, first serve. However, since the market orders are used almost exclusively by retail traders, the big players do not care, but the fight takes place in the limit orders and there the big players have a clear advantage. You will only get into the market faster in the limit area, compared to a market order, if it is an area that is not decisive for the big players. Therefore, market orders for retail traders could actually enable faster market entry. It is crucial to enter the market with a big player at the same time before pushing the price up or down. Identify iceberg orders

Hello dear subscribers,

In the last year I have dealt very intensively with the stock exchange data and specific filter settings of a corresponding software. In over 3000 hours I compared all possible chart settings with different filters. Some chart views have proven their worth, and I want to go into them today.

As we know, there is a long-term, medium-term and short-term price analysis that help us traders. In the past, I was very happy to use a H4 or D1 chart to get an overview of the long-term price trend. Since I usually work with key candles to identify a possible turnaround, it usually worked well, but in many cases I was extremely wrong. The main reason for this is the current market situation. In order for the big players to work efficiently in this market, the retail traders must always be exactly in the opposite position of the big players. As soon as a large number of retail traders act in the same direction as the big players, they are forced to react.

A nice example was created on February 20, 2019. The big players had already collected a large number of limit sell orders to push the price into the gap that was still open at the time. However, the majority of retail traders also assumed this and positioned themselves short. That's why the big players sold their short positions to retail traders at short notice, built up ASK positions at the same time and then pushed the price up sharply. Here you can read the article again:

Strong Buy Limits on Thursday

At the time, I could have sworn the price would go lower to close the open gap, but the big players used February 20 to switch positions. For me this is a crucial point why a long-term price forecast can never work. While many retail traders are looking for the least resistance, the big players do the opposite. You are looking for the path of greatest resistance, because the more retail traders are short, the more an upward movement is worthwhile in order to obtain the necessary liquidity. And since you can't determine from the outset how retail traders will position themselves during the day, a long-term price movement for me is a forecast with too much uncertainty.

The long-term course analysis can be compared, for example, with a map of Germany. I compare the medium-term course analysis with a navigation device and the short-term course analysis is while driving, the current view through the windshield. Since the long-term course analysis brings too much uncertainty, I would like to concentrate exclusively on the navigation device (medium-term price analysis) and the view through the windshield (short-term price analysis) in order to efficiently achieve my goal. I have now sorted my most efficient chart views according to this.

Medium-term course analysis

In addition to the open interest and the cumulative delta, a special footprint chart that focuses on the limit order and a limit delta chart that we have spoken about a few times help me.

Short-term price analysis

The respective strength of the different market orders and limit orders quickly show a trader the current market situation. I have already written about this in detail:

Act in the eye of the tornado

The headmap is a quick way to identify big player algorithms, and you also get specific information about what is happening in the current market. Here you can find the article:

Identification of the big player algorithms

The fastest price changes are only possible in the DOM and with a time and sales list. So I focus almost exclusively on these two elements. On April 19, 2020, I showed you specifically how the big players withdraw their limit orders in order to move the price extremely in one direction with a small number of market orders. Here you can find the article:

Which is stronger, market orders or limit orders?

This is the well-known spoofing, which you should definitely take a closer look at to identify short-term price changes. I would like to show you a specific example that I also deposited with a video.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

In this example we consider a small trend change (12 pip) after a stronger uptrend of 30 pip. In the video we see the movements that took place within the yellow rectangle. The price movements were not too strong at the time because initially a larger equilibrium was formed for the next 2 hours.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

As I have already shown a few times, the market sell orders (point A) run into the limit buy orders (point B). Behind the limit buy orders are the invisible iceberg oders (point C), which are added or subtracted from the limit buy orders as required. The market buy orders (point D) run into the limit sell orders (point E). Behind the limit sell orders are the invisible iceberg orders (point F), which are added or subtracted from the limit sell orders as required. For this I use a spoofing display from the DOM, which shows me the accumulated and current spoofing. Spoofing is all about how many limit orders have been added or subtracted in the waiting position, in the DOM. Special algorithms are used to facilitate identification.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Now let's start with the video sequence just before the course went down. In the M1 Forex display (Point A), it initially looks as if the price continues to go up. We can see that stronger positions were added in the area of limit buy orders (point B), while positions were subtracted in the area of limit sell orders (point C). This information initially indicates an upward movement. This is contradicted by the strength of the limit sell orders (point D), which is significantly higher than the strength of the limit buy orders (point E). At the same time, we recognize that the strength of the market sell orders (point F) is significantly greater than the strength of the market buy orders (point G). Overall, there was a short upward movement, but this was intercepted by the stronger limit sell orders. This clearly speaks for a downward movement.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Now the course begins to run downwards (Point A). We see that strong sell limit orders were added in spoofing (point B), while limit buy orders were withdrawn (point C). The limit sell orders (point D) and the market sell orders (point F) are significantly stronger. than the Limit Buy Orders (Point E) and Market Buy Orders (Point G). This clearly speaks for a further downward movement.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

At Point A we see that the course is trying to go up. However, spoofing points C and B speak against it. The limit sell orders (point D) are much too strong and there are no current market buy folders. Although these could come into the market at any time, the weakness of the limit buy orders speaks against the fact that further market buy orders come into the market. The strength of the market sell orders (point F) is significantly greater than the strength of the market buy orders (point G). That speaks for a further downward movement.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

We now see the reaction to our previous analysis. We recognize, that further limit sell orders are added (point C), while at point B more limit buy orders are deducted. The Limit Sell Orders (Point D) and Market Sell Orders (Point F) are significantly stronger than the Limit Buy Orders (Point E) and Market Buy Orders (Point G). --- 帖子 #1444 ---
While the formulas below offer a simple definition for icebergs, the most important characteristics is actually the gradual refreshing or stacking of the limit liquidity, never showing the full size of the intended position . Many believe it is this specific behavior that is associated with the building of a new position as opposed to exiting of a old position, which is also normally done via limit orders.

Bullish Iceberg:

Bid Volume > (10 * Average Bid depth) and Bull candle close

Bearish Iceberg:

Ask Volume > (10 * Average Ask depth) and Bear candle close

Note: some would consider the above a simple absorption and reserve the term iceberg for a significantly larger event 20X - 50X the average liquidity.

--- 帖子 #1447 ---
20% of the total volume are iceberg orders

Hello Nik,

An iceberg order is a limited buy or sell order on a stock exchange where the actual volume is not visible in the open order book, but only a small fraction of it. In addition to the total number of pieces, the peak number of pieces is defined for the iceberg order, which corresponds to the visible part of the order. After they have been fulfilled, another order with the same peak volume automatically moves in until the entire order volume has been fulfilled. This means that an iceberg order is only effective at one price level. The CME only supports two types of iceberg orders: native and synthetic.

Native iceberg orders are managed by the exchange itself. All new tranches are treated as modifications of the first order, so that the original order number is retained throughout the term of the iceberg order.

Synthetic iceberg orders are submitted by independent software providers whose infrastructure is physically separate from the exchange. These software providers split the original iceberg order, submit new tranches and track their execution. These tranches are indistinguishable from the usual limit orders of other participants.

Recognizing native iceberg orders is much easier because the order number only changes when the iceberg order has been fully processed. The big players work exclusively with synthetic iceberg orders in the stock market, which makes identification much more difficult.

A very complex analysis was carried out 8 months ago in the S&P 500 to identify iceberg orders and investigate them further. The algorithms used for this achieved an accuracy of 68%.

Result: Around 20% of the total trading volume is accounted for by iceberg orders, which can rise to 52% depending on the market situation and market environment. Over 50% of synthetic iceberg orders were canceled before they were fully executed. The synthetic iceberg orders use an average of 4 -5 tranches with an average peak of 4-5 lots. The average total volume of complete synthetic iceberg orders is between 10 and 20 lots. It is interesting to mention that the order sizes are often a multiple of 5, such as B. 10, 15 or 20.

The iceberg orders you mentioned, with a massive absorption, we find increasingly in the stock markets, they also occur in the EURUSD, but primarily through the provision of own volume. This is because in most cases the big players will only find enough volume at one price level if they are triggered stops from traders and some institutional traders, since the big players work without stops. However, stops have the peculiarity of being at different price levels, which is why the big players are forced to occupy multiple price levels with their iceberg orders in order to absorb the decisive volume of the stops. The result of many analysts who have dealt intensively with iceberg orders in recent years shows that we are dealing almost exclusively with smaller iceberg orders of 10-20 lots. That also coincides with our experience. Smaller iceberg orders are permanently abandoned in the EURUSD to hide the real interest in certain price levels in the DOM. So we have to assume that a number of iceberg orders were used in my video.

Identify iceberg orders

At the moment we have about 35 lot limit orders on one price level in the DOM, before the corona crisis we were around 70 lot per price level. This initially shows that there are significantly fewer big players on the market, which is understandable due to the quarantine regulations. The volume, on the other hand, remained the same, which resulted in higher volatility, since the limit orders could be broken faster. In this case in particular, the big players have to resort to iceberg orders to hide their interest in certain price levels.

Visible limit orders and invisible iceberg orders can only take up as much volume as the market currently provides. I see that immediately in the DOM, the time and sales list and with my liquidity profile. I absolutely agree that orders executed represent the true market situation, but at this moment that is already the past. No future forecasts can be derived from this.

Limit orders are added and deleted permanently, whereby either limit sell orders are deleted and limit buy orders are added, or limit sell orders are added and limit buy orders are deleted. In connection with the strength of the market orders and limit orders, this is the fastest way for me as a scalper to predict future movements with a very high degree of probability. We know that at CME, cumulative limit orders in the queue are given priority. This leads to the conclusion that identified, cumulative limit orders are always as close as possible to price execution. Spoofing is therefore a reliable way of optimally identifying future price defenses.

We recognize the tremendous power that the limit orders have in the market, which is why we will deal with them even more intensively over the next few months. The reason why so many traders lose is due to the ignorance of these things. To achieve a goal, we need to be able to identify the path. Together we can achieve that faster.

Spoofing algorithms

Hello dear subscribers,

As we already know, long-term price forecasts are not reliable and certainly cannot be read from candles. Since the big players only need the volume of retail traders and institutional traders, a current price trend is always dependent on their trading behavior. While the big players focus more on limit orders, the majority of retail traders work more with market orders. So my priority is more on limit orders.

In the DOM we can see ten levels of limit sell orders and limit buy orders. In earlier stock market times, these limit levels were a very reliable indicator of possible trend reversals, but the more market participants took advantage of this situation, the more difficult it became for the big players. In the nineties, the high-frequency traders then demonstrated how you can make a lot of money with deception. The big players then adopted some tricks from these high-frequency traders and use these tricks today to give the market a wrong picture of supply and demand.

We often experience in the market that there is an above-average number of lots at a certain limit level, which suggests to the market that the price will not be passed there. First the course runs to this zone and cannot break through it. Since the large order is not withdrawn, the market takes it seriously and now more short traders come into the market, which push the price down further. Potential long traders will exit this zone because they fear the price will go down. First the stops of the remaining long traders are triggered and the price accelerates downwards. The big player uses these stops to get out of the dollar that he has taken up with his large limit sell order. In addition, he can also sell his position to the other short traders who are now entering the market. With an invisible iceberg order, the big player stops the price down and pushes the price back up. Now the stops of the short traders are triggered and further accelerate the price. We had a similar situation this morning in EURUSD, which we will take a closer look at shortly.

First of all, this means that the visible limit orders in the DOM are not a reliable indicator in order to be able to do concrete trading transactions, since we never know whether a large visible limit order in the market is just a fake or real. Another problem is the iceberg orders, which are hidden behind the limit orders. Of course you can identify an iceberg order, but only after it has been executed. My approach, which I have been following for a few weeks, is to identify this iceberg order beforehand. In advance, that's basically possible, but the challenge is that we can only see ten price levels in the limit area. The big players are smart enough to set up their iceberg orders beforehand, so that there are certain difficulties with my idea. But there are also solutions for this.

--- 帖子 #1452 ---
The interplay of algo

Hello dear subscribers,

For hundreds of years, traders have been trying to identify patterns in prices or candles in order to derive them. All attempts to date have failed and there is no decisive starting point that is worth pursuing. The most common indicator used is without a doubt the moving average. Basically, a moving average is an instrument to identify market trends, but it is a lagging indicator. He can only display a trend after it has developed and he also shows a trend that has long since ended. This automatically brings delayed market insights. The price is the result of volume and liquidity, this information is not available in Forex. Basically, all indicators are lagging behind the price, so you can not expect an advantage for a better trading decision.

The probability of winning is 1:19 in the Forex market and 1: 6 in the Future market. This means that you get a 3 times better chance of winning with stock market data. This also results in a different distribution of profits. In the Future Market, 1 winner receives the losses of 6 losers, while in the Forex Market the winner receives the losses of the 19 losers. In addition, the forex market is over 100 times larger than the future market. The Future Market offers the greatest chance of winning, the Forex Market the best profit distribution. This results in a clear result: You should trade in the Forex market, but only on the basis of the future data. I have already described this procedure in great detail in this blog.

There are 5 times as many price movements in the Forex market, because one pip (10 pipettes) corresponds to 2 ticks in the future market. Therefore, the Forex market is much more sensitive to identify the key candle for a possible Stophunting with the help of my Bionic candle and the calculation of the ZigZag movements. In addition, the currency strength in Forex is a very efficient tool, but it should be adjusted to get quick information. We do not receive this important information in the stock market.

In the future market, the heat map, the DoM, the time and sales list, the spread tape, the limit market profile and a specially filtered limit footprint chart are among my favorites. With the appropriate settings and filtering, these views enable very quick market information to identify trend reversals properly.

Exchanges have existed for over 600 years and during this period many millions of traders have searched for concrete model processes. Even with the start of computer technology, innumerable programs and indicators were developed to research these patterns. So far, no special samples have been identified in the price that were able to provide a reliable price forecast. This fact alone prompted me to look for other ways that have not yet been explored.

That was the reason why I took a closer look at the algorithms of the big players. So far we have been able to identify some patterns that have always been similar, but we still need a lot of time to get closer to these algorithms. The results so far are much more efficient than working with indicators in the Forex market. The big players determine the market, use the limit orders for their entries and exits and need market orders to push the market in their desired direction. In order to fill their limit orders, they are always looking for the volume that can be most efficiently found in the stops of retail traders. With the help of the iceberg orders, the big players are able to add further limit orders unnoticed and thus collect or submit ask and bid. Interestingly, the average of iceberg orders is between 10 to 20 lots and not, as we previously thought, with an extremely high number of lots. Of course, there are also extreme absorptions, but they only come about because a big player makes volume available to himself. The iceberg orders were examined very extensively by different analysts, and it turned out that iceberg orders accounted for 20-50% of the total turnover. Many small iceberg orders at different price levels make it difficult to precisely identify absorption and continue to help big players dominate the market undetected.

Using algorithms, big players are able to completely remove sell limit orders from the market and at the same time push the price up with market buy orders. With this, you manage to move the market significantly with few market buy orders. This process is a permanent interplay and the algorithms are programmed exactly on it. Only now do I realize how extremely complex these algorithms are programmed. This process is very efficient and I would like to use a very simple example to illustrate this procedure.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

For the example described here, we assume that an accumulation of a big player has taken place at a lower price level than 1.10050, where he has collected a larger number of ask. After that, the price went up.

Point A

We are now at price level 1.10050 and the big player wants to push the price higher. While the price moved up from 1.09995, the big player algorithms ensured that the price levels 1.10050 to 1.10100 were filled with iceberg orders. As we know, larger limit orders are treated preferentially at CME. This ensures that the big player is the first in the queue at these levels. Of course, it cannot be prevented that there are still a few smaller orders from other market participants in between. The algorithms ensure that there are a number of different limit orders in the DoM, in our case between 25 and 55 lots. This is inconspicuous and nobody is suspicious. Behind it are larger iceberg orders, which can be added at any time. Now you have to ask yourself why the big player places a higher number of sell limit orders at precisely these price levels if he wants to push the price higher. Let's take a closer look at that.

Point B

The price is still at level 1.10050 and initially the big player hedges the price down by placing two larger iceberg orders at price levels 1.10045 and 1.10040. If a larger participant enters the market at this moment and invests a large number of market sell orders, the iceberg orders would absorb these market orders. Let us once again state that the big player has collected a large number of ask at a lower price level and would like to push the price higher in order to make it profitable. Therefore, the absorption of further questions at these two price levels would not be a disadvantage.

Point C

The big player suspects the first decisive stops of short traders from price level 1.10090. The algorithms ensure that all limit orders are deleted first.

Point D

At the same time, the algorithms now ensure that market buy orders are invested in order to overcome the remaining limit sell orders. The big player is thus able to go through a total of 9 price levels with just 38 lots. If these limit sell orders had not previously been placed in the market, he would have needed around 380 lots to go through these 9 price levels.

Point E

Now the first short trader stops are triggered and a chain reaction begins. Each stop triggers another stop and the price moves up. As a result of this strong upward price movement, further buyers are entering the market who are hoping for a further upward movement. The more long traders come into the market, in an upward movement, the less profitable it becomes for the big player. These long traders must therefore be switched off regularly.

Point F

The big player has already assigned price sell levels 1,10090 - 1,10040 with limit sell orders (iceberg orders). The big player absorbs the stops of the short traders (buy market orders) that are now triggered with his limit sell orders. We can now see that hardly stops were triggered at price level 1.10125 and the big player no longer suspects any more stops at the higher price levels. Starting at price level 1.10130, there are larger iceberg orders that are intended to prevent an upward price trend. The big player has now absorbed around 250 Lot Market Buy orders.

Point G

Here we see the price hedge of the big player again to hedge the ramping down price. In addition, he needs these iceberg orders to delete them at the crucial moment, when he wants to push the course down again.

Point H

The larger iceberg orders at levels 1.10130 and 1.10135 initially remain in the market in order to prevent a further price trend. The market is now realizing that a push up is impossible and the number of buyers is drastically reduced.

Point I

Now the big player wants to push the price down again to switch off the long traders and at the same time sell off his 250 lots of dollars at a lower price level. The quickest way to do this is to trigger the long trader stops.

Point J

First, he deletes his limit buy orders previously placed on the market so that he can push the price down with just a few market sell orders.

Point K

After the algorithms delete limit buy orders, they start investing some market sell orders. The big player suspects that the long trader's first stops should be at price level 1,10075. The price is now going down.

Point L

The first stops are triggered at price level 1,10075 and a chain reaction begins again. We now see large iceberg orders on the Limit Buy page that absorb these stops. First the big player gets out of the dollar with 250 lots, the absorption afterwards ensures a purchase of the euro. Thus, the big player can buy the euro again at a lower price level. At price level 1,10030, stronger iceberg orders are on the market again, which prevent a further drop in prices. All other market sell orders are now absorbed at this level. Then the price is pushed up again and the stops of the short traders help the big player to get the price up faster.

This described process of a pullback, within an upward movement, is of course much faster in reality and the algorithms are coordinated with one another in a thousandth of a second. At the same time, they coordinated to market buy / market sell orders and limit sell orders / limit buy orders. In principle, the process is always the same and a crucial point is that retail traders always place their stop above the last high or below the last low. The algorithms also use Fibonacci Zones, Moving Average, RSI and MACD to identify stops, as many retail traders use them. Of course, the big players have been able to gain a lot of experience in the past few decades in order to identify exactly large stop zones.

The procedure I have described is actually much more complicated and much more precisely coordinated. This is only a trading algorithm. There are also many other algorithms that, for example, search the market for hidden stops and report the results to the main computer. Pinging and snipping are used. The different approaches were taken over in part by the high-frequency traders. You can find more information here:

MAD World

Of course, artificial resistance zones are also created in the course of the price in order to entice retail traders to make investments that they would not otherwise have made. The obvious resistance zones that we find in the market did not come about by accident, but were deliberately initiated by the big players in order to make it easier to stop out the retail traders.

With this approach alone, it should be clear to everyone at the latest that news or meetings do not move the course or influence it dramatically. News and meetings are used by the big players to steer their project in the decisive direction, as there is a higher volatility at this time. However, an accumulation or distribution must have taken place beforehand, where the big player has collected a higher number of ask or bid. If no accumulation or distribution has taken place before, the price in an equilibrium only moves back and forth very much. It is therefore important to monitor these collection campaigns with the Limit Profile.

As we know, the big players are informed about everything before the news is published. They know the market like no one else and can therefore best estimate how a market will react to this information. Accumulation and distribution phases are then coordinated beforehand. The price trend is in principle only a reaction of the big players to the current situation in the market. If the big players have collected bids in a distribution phase and the majority of retail traders are also short-oriented, the big players will reorient themselves in the short term. They will sell their collected bid to retail traders and drive the price up. This is exactly what happened in EURUSD on February 19 and 20.

Volume always attracts liquidity!

The big players collect the individual stops of the retail traders with their limit orders. It is a permanent process in the market. If a price moves higher, we can assume that the majority of retail traders are short and vice versa. For this reason, a long-term price forecast is not possible because we never know from the outset how the majority of traders orient themselves in the long term. The price is only the result of volume and liquidity. The volume (stops of retail traders) automatically attracts liquidity. It is therefore absolutely logical and understandable that there can be no clear patterns within the price. Likewise, there are no clear patterns in the area of bid and ask. But there are clear patterns in the area of algorithms that are responsible for the correspondence between liquidity and volume. This is exactly why my views are geared towards examining this correspondence of the algorithms in more detail.

The Forex volume is wrong

Hello dear subscribers,

In recent years there have been more and more trainers and companies who have jumped on the “Volume Trader” train to make a lot of money. Then programmers came onto the market that enabled footprint charts and volume profiles in the forex market. Young traders who have not worked with charts like this before were impressed and saw this as an opportunity to improve their trading opportunities. When I first saw a footprint chart and a volume profile, I also thought that these representations are a guarantee of success. I can assure you that the opposite is true, because the volume is of no use to us in the Forex market. There is only the possibility for institutional traders to get a correct volume.

If you add up the number of lots, ask and bid, the volume results. The volume is the total turnover of market buy orders and market sell orders. With the volume, we can see at which price levels there has been a major battle between buyers and sellers, that's all. We cannot tell from the volume whether the buyer or seller side was stronger. For this you have to be able to distinguish between bid and ask. There is no bid and ask depicted in the Forex market, so we should ask ourselves the question of how to generate volume at all? The volume in the forex market is generated via the ticks. Let's first look at what a tick is exactly.

In principle, a tick is a trading transaction, whereby it does not matter whether only 1 lot or 100 lots are traded in this trading transaction. To make ticks visible, there is the possibility to work with a tick chart. A tickchart is a time-independent chart, in which you determine after how many trades a period has ended. A new candle is drawn in a 64 tick chart after 64 trades. This has the advantage that more candles are drawn at high volatility and fewer candles are created at lower volatility. A disadvantage, candle formations are not identifiable, ou shouldn't work with that anyway. It is striking that the volume in a tick chart is approximately the same, making it more difficult to analyze volume spikes. Here you can find a detailed article about the calculation of the Forex volume:

Volume in forex

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Here we see a tick chart in the Euro FX from the future market. The yellow line denotes 1 lot within a trade. The average number of trades is larger than one lot, but the chart was created 1.5 hours after the London Open. As a rule, the number of lots within a trade is significantly lower.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

At Point A we see a 10,000 tick chart, which means that a new candle is automatically formed after 10,000 trades. Ask and bid is invested within the individual candles, which then leads to the total volume (point B). At point C, I divided the volume by the number of ticks. This results in the diagram at Point D. Basically, the number of lots must always be equal to or greater than the trading transactions. Because a trade always contains at least one lot. In our calculation, a trade has an average of 1.46 lots, although no general derivation can be drawn from it, since the values fluctuate massively.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Now we compare the volume Forex / Future, each in an H4 chart. First of all, there are certain deviations in the H4 candles, but this has to do with the respective stock exchange opening times. Overall, it is striking that the volume in the forex chart is not comparable to the volume in the future chart. So there seems to be a different calculation. We now want to take a closer look at this.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

First, let's refer to the numbers that we know are correct.

Point A

In Forex EURUSD we know that about $ 2 trillion in sales are traded each day. However, these values fluctuate. One lot is worth $ 100,000, which means around 20 million lots are traded per day. In recent years, an average of 92,160 ticks per day have been achieved in EURUSD. According to my broker's information, these values relate exclusively to the sales of this broker. Overall, the result would mean that an average of 217 lots would be traded per trade. That is a value that I strongly doubt. Therefore, we want to take a closer look at these ticks in the Forex market in order to find the most realistic value possible.

Point B

In the future market, the values are clear, from the stock market data. An average of $ 18 billion is traded per day, which is the average lots (144,000) multiplied by the lot value of $ 125,000. 98,630 ticks have been reached on average per day in recent years. This means that a trade deal averaged 1.46 lots. This number is logical and understandable for me.

Point C

The forex market is approximately 100 times larger than the future market, with daily fluctuations being completely normal. In this context, the ratio of lots per day is understandable in both markets. At first glance, the lot / tick / pip ratio is understandable, which, however, is not correct in my opinion. I came to the conclusion that the number of ticks is similar in both markets. In my view, the number in the Forex market cannot be correct, for the following reasons. The Forex market is much more volatile, because the smallest movement is expected in pipettes . If the price changes by one pip, the price has to go through ten different levels. In the future market, the price has to go through only two stages at the same time. This fact automatically means that a significantly higher number of ticks would have to be generated in the forex market than in the future market.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The volume is nothing more than a summary of ask and bid. However, no bid and ask is passed on in the forex market, but this is a crucial point that a trader needs. This means that ask and bid do not fight against each other and are not able to influence each other. The decisive factor is whether liquidity lets these market orders through or absorbs and stops them. As we know, the big players primarily work with liquidity. Hi Micha

I agree with you that passive limit orders move the market and I also agree the Algo is selective in which limit orders it chooses to open.

For example if the market is rising and hits a deep pool of liquidity and plans a bearish move, if you place a a limit Sell order in the area of thin liquidity, perhaps say at the top edge of the pool, there is only a 50% the Algo will step up to open the order.  If now we change that limit sell order to a Buy limit order and place it at the say spot, it will almost always open up the losing position.

That is what I see on a live chart trading around liquidity pools and it really does feel like your small retail order goes to the back of the queue and not to be touched, unless it suits the market makers. My stats say 2 to 1, it will only open a order that suits them.

This is why I no longer use passive limit orders and stops but choose to sit on my chart while a position is opened.  One trick I do see the Algo perform a lot on M1 chart is to produce a wide ranging candle of say 8 pips, hold movement for 2-3 seconds then create a tiny gap up and move about half a pip.   It gives the sense price is moving bullish.  It then holds for another 2-3 seconds allowing time for those traders to jump in with market buy orders - Then goes strongly bearish.

Time & Time again.

So placing passive Limit orders on a chart gives only a moderate advantage to the retail trader unless they are can't be on the charts at the time, in my opinion.

Cheers Rick

Pattern search in the algorithms

Hello dear subscribers,

Since the beginning of February 2020, we have been working intensively on the algorithms of the big players, which are primarily responsible for a smooth process and optimal communication between the market and the limit orders. Limit orders are used to collect ask and bid in accumulation and distribution phases, to exit positions and to hold the price. Market orders are used to start the first stops of retail traders, to push a price into a certain zone and to make volume available to yourself.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

The market sell orders run in the limit buy orders (point A) and the market buy orders run in the limit sell orders (point B). First of all, we should consider these two movements separately. At point C we see a footprint chart, on the left we see the market sell orders and on the right the market buy orders. 24 lot market sell orders and 129 lot market buy orders were traded in the largest volume range. But these two market orders have nothing to do with each other because they never meet in the market. Therefore, one should look at the movements separately.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Regardless of whether we analyze a bullish or bearish candle, the price always runs in ZigZag movements down or up. First and foremost, it is all about getting the necessary volume to achieve the respective goals of the big players. The herd plays a crucial role in this. The big players achieve the highest profits when the masses are oriented in exactly the opposite direction to their investments.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

Limit orders actually move the market because they are mainly used by big players in the form of small iceberg orders. The background is that these iceberg orders are not displayed in the DoM and it is very difficult to specifically identify these invisible orders. The big players are thus able to disguise their actual intentions and thus have a decisive advantage. While most traders are looking for directions in the dark, the big players work with a night vision device. You see us, we don't see them. This is a crucial point that brings big players over $ 400 million in profit every day.

Upward movements should be calculated separately from downward movements. A footprint chart or a candle is the worst way to display these movements correctly. What is much more important in a downward movement is how the market sell orders meet the limit buy orders. Can the market sell orders break the limit buy orders or are they stopped? If market sell orders are held up, it means someone is buying Ask. Ask is used to buy the euro or to exit the dollar. It is difficult to predict a subsequent upward trend from this, as it could only be a partial exit. The price will continue to go down after the partial exit as the main positions are still in the market. So you have to keep an eye on the overall situation. The past course of the course only plays a subordinate role, since the big players are always oriented towards the current situation. The herd is always decisive, the big players must always take an opposite position. If the herd behavior suddenly changes, the big players must also adapt to the new situation. The big players are basically the herds slaves. The herd always determines the course of the course and not the big players. When the herd takes a short position, the big players push the price up and vice versa. Of course, the big players always win because they can use more money, but the herd sets the direction. And since you can never estimate how the herd of one million retail traders will react tomorrow or next week in EURUSD, long-term price forecasting is impossible. In contrast, assessing the big players is much easier. The identification of the algorithms help me to look into the future for a few seconds. The shorter I am in the market, the higher my probability of winning, but the less effective the costs are. Optimal profit management must be created from this.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

A simple derivation can be created from the procedure of the big players and retail traders. The retail traders primarily use the market orders. The market orders are displayed exactly in the market. The position of the retail trader can be determined from this. The art now is to know that this is the wrong direction. To win, you have to take an opposite position at the right time. This is possible with the big player reaction. Stophunting is a crucial point to analyze a specific market behavior, so I recommend every trader to deal with it in more detail.

In the picture we see a situation where a big player has made volume available to himself, that he has also taken up with own limit sell orders. First the price was pushed down 40 pip and within one equilibrium the big player got out of the dollar. After that he started buying the euro and pushed the price back down to the price level where he gave himself liquidity. From this price level, the price then went up 70 pip. Through his own liquidity he made 40 pip profits with the dollar and 70 pip profits with the euro. With the euro that he bought in the Equilibrium, he was able to realize a profit of 110 pip. It only took him 28 hours to do this. The volatility was relatively low at this point and the decision to provide liquidity was absolutely right at this point as the market did not provide such volume at this price level.

I would like to come back to slide number 3 and go into the two different movements. Regardless of whether it is an upward or downward movement, it is primarily controlled by limit orders. The limit orders are significantly stronger than the market orders, here you find the report.

Which is stronger, market orders or limit orders?

No matter how many market orders come in, if a big player keeps adding new iceberg orders, the price will never be able to break through this price level.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)

We can compare this principle with a dam. The water is supposed to represent the market orders and the lock gate at point A are the limit orders. If the lock gate is closed, the water can run against it, but the lock gate will always stop the water. There are now two dams on the market, one for the upward course and one for the downward course. If the price is to go up, the lock gate on the limits sell orders must be opened and at the same time the lock gate on the limits buy orders must be closed so that the water cannot run back. The Big Player algorithms must simultaneously control the lock opening and the water flow in both directions. And exactly the algorithms of this controller I try to analyze with different stock market data. For this I use different filter settings in the DoM, the heat map and the time and sales list.

Attached Image (click to enlarge)
